- Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21; week1-lecture.md p.46]

## Conditioning and energy systems

- Conditioning is defined two ways: (1) how well an athlete can meet the energy requirements of their specific sport/activity, and (2) how well they sustain strength, speed, and power output across a full competition. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.22]
- All three energy systems (alactic ~10-12s highest power, glycolytic/anaerobic-lactic ~60-90s medium capacity, aerobic hours-long lowest power/highest capacity) are always active simultaneously; programming targets the adaptation, not the drill label. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.19; class-4-2026.md p.15]
- A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once — priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands (e.g., for football: prepared for fall camp first, then the first game). **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31]
- For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39]
- Anaerobic (lactate) threshold heart-rate zones are assigned by athlete body size rather than a single number: roughly 165 bpm for big/tall athletes, 170 for medium, 175 for small, with Zone 1-4 bands set as percentages of that individual threshold. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.28-29]
- The traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest — this ordering is used to sequence what needs the most frequent re-exposure. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.47]
- Training intensities between roughly 75-90% of maximal effort are labeled (via Francis) "no man's land" — too fast to build alactic power cleanly, too slow to build real aerobic capacity — and are treated as a zone to generally avoid as a primary training target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.48]
- "Everything we do is some form of conditioning": lifting, agility work, and skill drills each load a specific energy system (power vs. capacity, alactic/glycolytic/aerobic) and should be classified and counted as conditioning, not treated as separate from it. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31, tables pp.35-42]
- For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity — a better-developed aerobic system means more available energy on play 10, 11, or 12 of a drive, not longer continuous running ability. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md p.9]
- Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.51; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]
- Joel Jamieson's *Ultimate MMA Conditioning* is recommended as the single best practical resource for energy-system development, on the basis that its methods transfer cleanly to non-combat sports despite the MMA framing. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md pp.49-50; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]

## Tensions and contradictions

1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.

2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.

3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.

4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.

5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.

6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]

7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.

8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.

9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.

10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.

19	- **Baseline:** back squat about **2.65× BW**; isometric mid-thigh pull **5.78× BW**. It is unclear whether that was single- or double-leg; the pull came before Natera moved to iso squats. CMJ about **59–62 cm**.
20	- **GPP:** eccentric calf work, then hip ISO holds progressing to switches.
21	- **SPP:** ankle and hip ISO catches, plus "ISO stadium descents," a loaded, cyclical isometric step-down that comes after the continuum.
22	- **Loads cited:** ankle ISO catch "up to 160 kg" (the transcript says "leaving up to 160 kilo"), which is implausible against his own 60 kg example and needs verifying on video. Hip ISO catch about 35 kg.
23	- **Reported changes:** CMJ +3 cm; CMJ power (~6,000 W) +200–300 W; takeoff velocity up; **RSI** "improved significantly," which he calls the main win; shorter contact times at about 30–40 m; longer acceleration and higher max velocity (around 11 m/s).
24	
25	**Female 100 m hurdler.** She was coached by a Polish coach whose name the ASR renders "Peter Marazu ski" (name unverified), with Natera collaborating. Her times stagnated in 2016–2017. Run-specific isometrics (RSI) were added in 2018 through mid-2019 alongside "track training" and traditional squats, deadlifts and Olympic lifts. She used **holds and pushes only**, and progressed past targets such as a **2× BW ankle hold**. Afterwards her hurdle times and speed improved to "elite level." Her quote to a reporter: "I don't lift heavy weights. I just hold them."
26	
27	*(Every number is single-source ASR from slides; the before/after charts are visual only. Verify at ~95:05–100:58.)*
28

In football that is the big, strong accelerator (RB/LB type) whose drop-jump RSI on ForceDecks is low for his strength. Track RSI and single-leg iso push together to see whether one moves without the other.
32

13	
14	# Strength Training Adapts Along (at Least) Ten Independent, Narrow Dimensions
15	
16	**What it is** — Strength gains transfer narrowly, not generally, across at least ten
17	independent dimensions: type of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region/range of
18	movement, velocity of movement, force of contraction, muscle fibre recruitment,
19	metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility, and fatigue. Training that improves one
20	dimension often produces little or no improvement on the others, even when the same
21	muscle groups are involved. Specificity is explicitly distinguished from simulation:
22	mimicking a sport movement with added resistance is not the same as training the specific
23	factors above, and can actually distort the neuromuscular programming needed for the real
24	skill because of changes in center of gravity, moment of inertia, and mechanical
25	stiffness introduced by the resistance. (PDF pp. 38-39, printed pp. 27-28.)
26	
27	**Why it works** — Strength adaptation is produced and expressed by the nervous and
28	muscular systems together (see
29	[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]); the specific
30	demands (velocity, joint angle, contraction type, metabolic pathway) shape which
31	recruitment patterns, fibre types, and biochemical pathways are trained, so a change in
32	any one of those parameters can produce a materially different, largely non-transferable
33	adaptation. This is one of the more broadly replicated findings in strength and
34	conditioning research, independent of this text.
35	
36	**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a master reasoning check before assuming an
37	exercise "transfers" to a sport skill: ask which of the ten dimensions the exercise
38	actually matches, not just whether it uses similar muscles. **Eric's baseline:** the
39	Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of
40	movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production,
41	and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise transfers, and
42	is taught in HHPR 5355 (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
43	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14`, `week1-lecture.md p.34`). **Inference:**
44	Dynamic Correspondence (this book's Ch4.3, not yet ingested) is plausibly the applied
45	extension of this same ten-dimension specificity logic to exercise selection, though this
46	chapter does not itself state that link.
47	
48	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't use "specificity" as an argument against any
49	general preparation work; this book's own 1.1 material and this library's Bompa
50	multilateral/LTAD entries support building a general base before narrowing to sport-specific
51	work. This principle governs which dimensions transfer, not whether general work has value
52	at an earlier training age; that distinction is this entry's own reading, not stated as
53	such in this passage of the text.
54	
55	**Example** — **Inference:** Heavy squat strength does not automatically transfer to high-velocity sprint
56	force production (different point on the velocity dimension) even though both use similar
57	musculature; each needs its own specific training exposure.
58	
59	**Related** — [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]],
60	[[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]].
61

12	---
13	
14	# Classic Energy-System Percentage Tables by Sport (Fox & Mathews, 1974) — Football Listed at ~90% Phosphagen
15	
16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky reproduces Fox & Mathews' (1974) classic tables estimating
17	the percentage contribution of the short-term (phosphagen/ATP-CP), intermediate
18	(non-oxidative glycolytic), and long-term (oxidative/aerobic) energy systems to different
19	training modes and sports. American football is listed at 90% short-term, 10%
20	intermediate, 0% long-term — among the most phosphagen-dominant sports in the table,
21	comparable to golf (95/5/0) and volleyball (90/10/0), and far more phosphagen-dominant
22	than field hockey or soccer half-backs (60/20/20). Verkhoshansky himself cautions that
23	this "highly determinate" scheme, compiled decades earlier, has been questioned, that
24	figures for some events (he names the 1500m specifically) have since been revised, and
25	that it should not be used casually because it disguises moment-to-moment metabolic
26	demand shifts within a single sport. (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81.)
27	
28	**Why it works** — The table estimates an average, whole-game contribution, whereas actual
29	play consists of short high-intensity bursts (plays) separated by long rest (huddles,
30	substitutions), so an average figure can obscure the real repeated-sprint, phosphagen-
31	dominant-per-play structure while also underweighting the role of aerobic recovery between
32	bursts.
33	
34	**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's stated conditioning priority for
35	football is alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp and game demands, with
36	glycolytic conditioning treated as a "worst case scenario" absorbed incidentally rather
37	than programmed as a primary target (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
38	systems," citing `class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39`); the baseline also states the aerobic
39	system's main value for speed-power athletes is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP
40	between bouts), not distance capacity (citing `2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md
41	p.9`). **Inference:** this table's 90/10/0 split for football (near-zero credited to the
42	long-term/aerobic system) looks, at first read, to be in tension with the baseline's
43	explicit inclusion of aerobic capacity as a Goal-1 priority for football — but the tension
44	likely resolves once "aerobic system" is understood functionally: the baseline treats
45	aerobic fitness as enabling faster ATP/phosphagen regeneration between the very
46	phosphagen-dominant plays this table describes, not as a source of in-play energy. Read
47	together, not as contradictory: this table describes what fuels a single play; the
48	baseline describes what determines how well that fuel regenerates for the next one.
49	
50	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky's own caution applies directly here: **Inference**
51	do not use the 90/10/0 football figure as a precise or current number; it is a decades-old
52	average estimate for the sport as a whole, not a modern, position-specific or play-by-play
53	breakdown, and the source text itself flags the whole table's accuracy as needing
54	re-examination. This entry is rated `contested` because it is presented as a classic,
55	already-questioned scheme rather than an established modern reference.
56	
57	**Example** — **Inference:** a single football play (a few seconds of maximal effort)
58	draws almost entirely on the phosphagen system, consistent with the table; but the
59	athlete's ability to repeat that near-maximal output play after play, series after series,
60	depends heavily on aerobic capacity for recovery between plays — the quality the baseline
61	prioritizes.
62	
63	**Related** — None in this ingest yet; candidate future link to a conditioning synthesis
64	note once Phase 4 of the Flint project reaches conditioning and energy systems.
65

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute
entries.description:
Run multiple commands in ONE call. Every command's output is auto-indexed into the knowledge base; if you also pass `queries`, the matching sections come back in the same round trip so a follow-up search call is not needed.

Concurrency parallelizes the FETCH phase (run-the-commands). The DERIVATION phase — turning raw output into an answer — still belongs in code: add a processing command that consumes the indexed output and prints only the answer, so the raw bytes never enter your conversation (Think-in-Code, same principle as the sandbox tool).

WHEN:
  - You have 3+ related commands you would otherwise run sequentially (multi-issue lookups, git log + git diff + git blame, multi-file reads, multi-region cloud queries)
  - You want to gather AND query in one round trip — pass `queries` so the matching sections come back inline
  - You want to parallelize I/O-bound work — pass `concurrency` 2-8 (network calls, gh CLI, cloud APIs, multi-repo git reads)
  - The combined output is large enough that piping it through ctx_search later would itself be expensive — let auto-index + inline queries do both in one shot

WHEN NOT:
  - Single command with no follow-up query — run it in the sandbox tool directly
  - CPU-bound or stateful commands — keep concurrency at 1 (npm test, build, lint, port-binding servers, lock-file holders, anything that races on the same resource)

RETURNS:
  Auto-indexed section list per command label, plus top matches per query (when `queries` is passed). Raw output is NOT echoed in full — only the matched windows. Concurrency>1 switches each command to its own per-command timeout (no shared budget); concurrency=1 preserves the legacy shared-budget cascading-skip-on-timeout path. Use 4-8 for I/O-bound batches; keep at 1 for CPU work or shared-state commands; lower the value when target hosts enforce per-IP rate limits.

EXAMPLE: ctx_batch_execute(
  commands: [
    {label: "issue 1", command: "gh issue view 1"},
    {label: "issue 2", command: "gh issue view 2"},
    {label: "summarize", command:… [truncated]

label.description: Section header for this command's output (e.g., 'README', 'Package.json', 'Source Tree')

commands.description: Commands to execute as a batch. Output is labeled with the section header. Default order is sequential; pass concurrency>1 to run in parallel (output stays in input order).

queries.description: Search queries to extract information from indexed output. Use 5-8 comprehensive queries. Each returns top 5 matching sections with full content. This is your ONLY chance — put ALL your questions here. No follow-up calls needed.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs. With concurrency=1, the value (when set) is a shared budget across commands; with concurrency>1, it is applied per-command.

concurrency.description: Max commands to run in parallel (1-8, default: 1). Use 4-8 for I/O-bound batches (network, gh, curl, multi-repo git reads). Keep at 1 for CPU-bound (npm test, build, lint) or stateful commands (ports, locks). >1 switches to per-command timeouts (no shared budget) and individual `(timed out)` blocks instead of cascading skip.

cwd.description: Optional working directory for all shell commands in this batch.

query_scope.description: Scope for `queries` (default: `batch`). `batch` searches ONLY the chunks produced by this batch's commands — useful when you want answers about the just-fetched output. `global` searches the entire persistent index (same scope as ctx_search) — useful when you want the batch commands to enrich context and the queries to also surface related prior knowledge in one round trip.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute

code.description: Source code to execute. Use console.log (JS/TS), print (Python/Ruby/Perl/R), echo (Shell), echo (PHP), fmt.Println (Go), IO.puts (Elixir), or Console.WriteLine (C#) to output a summary to context.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs (which is the right layer for this policy). Pass an explicit value for long-running builds (Gradle/Maven/SBT).

background.description: Keep process running after timeout (for servers/daemons). Returns partial output without killing the process. IMPORTANT: Do NOT add setTimeout/self-close timers in background scripts — the process must stay alive until the timeout detaches it. For server+fetch patterns, prefer putting both server and fetch in ONE ctx_execute call instead of using background.

cwd.description: Optional working directory for shell commands. Non-shell languages still execute from their sandbox temp directory.

intent.description:
What you're looking for in the output. When provided and output is large (>5KB), indexes output into knowledge base and returns section titles + previews — not full content. Use ctx_search(queries: [...]) to retrieve specific sections. Example: 'failing tests', 'HTTP 500 errors'.

TIP: Use specific technical terms, not just concepts. Check 'Searchable terms' in the response for available vocabulary.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file
entries.description:
Read a file into a sandboxed FILE_CONTENT variable and run code over it. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation — the file bytes stay in the sandbox.

Think-in-Code applied to file-level analysis: Reading the whole file means every byte enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session. Running code over it here lets you keep the raw bytes out and only the derived answer in. Same principle as ctx_execute, scoped to one named file via the FILE_CONTENT variable.

WHEN:
  - You want to KNOW SOMETHING ABOUT a file (line count, matches of a pattern, parsed structure, statistical aggregate) without needing to SEE all of it
  - The file is structured (CSV, JSON, log, code) and a code-level derivation is cheaper than reading verbatim
  - The file is large enough that reading the full content would burn meaningful conversation memory you need for the actual work
  - The derivation may itself produce a large output you want recall-by-topic on later — pass an `intent` string; outputs over ~5KB are auto-indexed and only matching sections come back, retrievable via ctx_search

WHEN NOT:
  - You intend to EDIT the file — use Read so the subsequent Edit can match the exact text
  - You only need one specific line and you know its offset — Read with offset/limit is the simplest path
  - The file is small AND you will consume all of it for understanding/editing — Read directly

RETURNS:
  Only what your code prints. The FILE_CONTENT variable holds the raw bytes inside the sandbox; nothing else leaves. When `intent` is set and output exceeds the auto-index threshold, the response carries searchable section titles + previews instead of the raw stdout.

EXAMPLE: ctx_execute_file(path: "huge.log", language: "javascript", code: "const errs = FILE_CONTENT.split('\\n').filter(l => /ERROR|FATAL/.test(l)); console.log(`${errs.length} error lines`); console.log(errs.slice(-5).join('\\n'))")
EXAMPLE: ctx_execute_file(path: "data.csv", language: "javascript", code: "const rows = FILE_CONTE… [truncated]

path.description: Absolute file path or relative to project root

code.description: Code to process FILE_CONTENT (file_content in Elixir). Print summary via console.log/print/echo/IO.puts/Console.WriteLine.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs.

intent.description: What you're looking for in the output. When provided and output is large (>5KB), returns only matching sections via BM25 search instead of truncated output.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search
entries.description:
Search a unified knowledge base with a multi-strategy ranking pipeline. Two parallel matchers run on every query: a Porter-stemming matcher ("caching" finds "cached", "caches", "cach") and a trigram-substring matcher ("useEff" finds "useEffect"). Their ranked lists are merged via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so a document that ranks well in both surfaces above one that wins only on a single strategy. Multi-term queries get an additional proximity-rerank pass that boosts passages where the query terms appear close together. Typos are corrected via Levenshtein distance and re-searched. Result snippets are window-extracted around the matched terms, not blindly truncated.

The knowledge base is unified: queries reach indexed content you stored (ctx_index, ctx_fetch_and_index, ctx_batch_execute output) AND auto-captured session memory written by hooks (decisions, errors, blockers, plans, user prompts, rejected approaches, tool failures, compaction guides — 26 event categories). File-backed sources carry a content hash and auto-flag staleness when the source file changes.

WHEN:
  - You want to recall something that exists in storage (recently indexed content, prior session events, auto-memory) instead of re-reading raw sources
  - You have multiple related questions about the same body of knowledge — batch every question into one call (the ranking pipeline runs per-query but the round-trip cost is paid once)
  - You want to scope the query to one labelled source (pass `source` — partial match is fine)
  - You want a chronological view across current session + prior sessions + persistent auto-memory (pass `sort: "timeline"` — the default `relevance` mode only ranks within the current session)
  - You want to filter ranked results by content shape (pass `contentType: "code"` to surface implementation snippets or `contentType: "prose"` to surface explanations)

WHEN NOT:
  - The data you want to query has never been stored in the knowledge base AND no session memory has accumulated around it — capture first (run a gather-and-… [truncated]

queries.description: Array of search queries. Batch ALL questions in one call.

source.description: Filter to a specific indexed source (partial match).

contentType.description: Filter results by content type: 'code' or 'prose'.

sort.description: Sort mode. 'relevance' (default): BM25 ranked, current session only. 'timeline': chronological across current session, prior sessions, and auto-memory.

project.description: Project scope. Default (omit): this session's project — auto-resolved from the host adapter. 'global': span every project in the shared store (cross-project recall). <absolute-path>: scope to that specific project directory.

1	===PAGE 106===
2	SUPERTRAINING
3	SPORT SPECIFIC  
4	STRENGTH TRAINING
5	Special Strength Training
6	Strength training has become vital for successful sports preparation. However, it is only of value if a specific 
7	methodology can be devised on the basis of scientific research, detailing the role and place of strength conditioning 
8	in the training process in the short and long term.
9	Regrettably, its historical links with physique training and the traditional view of muscle-bound gymnasium 
10	patrons have created the faulty impression that strength training retards athletic performance. Current emphasis 
11	on research into heart disease and cardiovascular physiology has served to consolidate this view by popularising 
12	the belief that fitness and cardiac health in general are well served by ’aerobic’ or cardiovascular exercise and 
13	endangered or minimally enhanced by training against resistance. The 'aerobics' community has confounded the 
14	picture further by empirically categorising many strength conditioning exercises as dangerous and generally 
15	regarding aerobic activity as superior to all other forms of exercise.
16	It often seems to be forgotten that fitness is a complex state determined by several interacting components 
17	(the fitness factors discussed in 1.14.3), each of which requires specialised training for optimal development. 
18	Strength processes play a particularly important role in controlling the stability and mobility of the body in sport.
19	Fortunately, a sizeable community of'strength scientists' has emerged to challenge the above preconceptions 
20	and examine the part played by strength and strength conditioning in human performance and injury rehabilitation. 
21	Some of their work is now revealing that muscle strength and endurance may play key roles in ensuring superior 
22	performance even during long duration events such as marathons. For instance, research into the biomechanics of 
23	the soft tissues has indicated that performance in distance running also may be enhanced by (Sifif, 1986):
24	• improving the ability of the SEC (series elastic component) of the muscle complex to store and release 
25	elastic energy
26	• modifying running technique to improve the ability of the athlete to utilise the stored elastic energy and to 
27	spare muscular energy.
28	As detailed in Chapter 1, the mechanical properties of connective tissues (such as elasticity, strength and damping 
29	ratio), as well as neuromuscular efficiency (discussed in later chapters), can be beneficially altered by using 
30	appropriate regimes of resistance and plyomctric training.
31	The striking success achieved by Russian and Eastern European coaches in applying specialised strength 
32	training in preparation for most sports has also stimulated the rest of the world to take this type of conditioning 
33	far more seriously. Considerable experience has now been gained in the use of special strength training to facilitate 
34	adequate analysis and identify some general principles. However, it has been insufficient to form a definitive 
35	methodological foundation for the special strength training of athletes. The role and place of special strength 
36	training can be established only through scientific research in two main directions:
37	• Further study of the principles governing the general  conditioning of the body to determine scientific means 
38	of achieving one's physical potential
39	• Intensive study of the principles determining the specific long-term sports training process.
40	Scicntific research in the first direction already has yielded a wealth of information, whereas serious work in the 
41	second direction has commenced only recently, so that its findings are still rather limited. Nevertheless, they 
42	enable one to formulate important principles concerning special strength training , where the latter term refers to 
43	the specialised application of strength training to sport. It is synonymous with sport specific strength training , 
44	and both expressions may be used interchangeably to distinguish it from general weight training or bodybuilding for 
45	aesthetic or casual fitness purposes.
46	At the outset, it must be emphasized that the phenomenon of strength should not be viewed simplistically in 
47	terms of the classical definition as 'the ability to produce force by action of the muscles'. Strength is highly context

50

53	SUPERTRAINING
54	dependent. This point will be stressed throughout this book, since strength can manifest itself in many forms, such 
55	as static strength, dynamic strength, strcngth-speed and strcngth-endurance. The accurate modelling of the 
56	strength and other fitness characteristics of a particular sport is what transforms general  strength training into 
57	special  strength training to produce consistent improvement in sports performance.
58	The Russian System of Classifying Athletes
59	Before going any further, it is relevant to remark on the use of the terms Sports Mastery  or Mastery in Sport. 
60	These terms have been used for many years in Russia and Eastern Europe to describe the process of reaching the 
61	highest possible level of sporting prowess.
62	They are also closely related to the categorisation scheme used to identify athletes of different qualification. 
63	In this scheme, competitors at the most basic level fall into Class III, athletes of intermediate standard into Class
64	II, and advanced athletes successively into Class I, Candidate for Master of Sport, Master of Sport, Candidate for 
65	International Master and International Master (or, Master of Sport, International Class). The last two categories 
66	refer to athletes such as world record holders, world champions and world champions of several years' standing. 
67	Specific norms are set for all individual and team sports, based on times, distances, scorcs, lifts, number of times of 
68	selection at a given team level or special achievements. The classification system does not rank beginners, since 
69	ranking is based on specific achievements.
70	It is one of the objectives of this book to present information which will assist the athlete to progress via the 
71	use of appropriate and effective strength training through all the stages of Mastery to the highest possible level 
72	dictated by his/her inherited potential.
73	It should be noted that the Russian system of classifying athletes begins not with formal competitions, but 
74	with the GTO (Readiness for Work and Defence) badge, which recognizes the minimum standards of physical 
75	fitness for anyone in the population. The GTO norms apply to children from about 10 years of age and progress 
76	into late adulthood (over 65 years of age). The GTO tests involve several sports and serve to identify levels of 
77	athletic prowess in the formative years. Those whose intention is to progress beyond the GTO IV, III, II and I 
78	badges have to pass more rigorous requirements to lead them through the various Classes of Mastery as detailed 
79	above. Before one reaches the adult classification system, there are also junior rankings (Class III up to Class I) foe 
80	athletes of up to 19 years.
81	The classification of athletes should not be regarded as a regimented system with strict application only in the 
82	Russian context, but a fundamental principle for the scientific preparation of athletes in all countries. Since 
83	athletes of different levels ofproficiency and training experience respond very differently to strength conditioning  
84	programmes , it is vital that competitors be periodically tested and graded to enable coaches to set up the most 
85	appropriate training regimen for each individual during a specific phase of development.
86	The Early Stages of Strength Training
87	A few remarks arc necessary about the early stages of strength training. Virtually any methods o f strength training  
88	will enhance the strength of a novice during the first few months , provided the intensity, in particular, is kept at a 
89	safe level. This is a major reason why it is misleading and counterproductive to apply the results obtained from 
90	scientific studies of less than at least six months' duration. It is also a major reason why relatively inexperienced 
91	coaches manage to have initial success with athletes and thereby continue to attract clients. Moreover, it has been 
92	discovered that each individual displays a different rate, degree and efficiency of responding to the same type,  
93	quality and quantity of physical training.  In other words, the identical training programme will have different 
94	effects on different people. The achievement of higher levels of mastery is a complex process which requires the 
95	careful application of the appropriate means and methods of training at the different stages of sports preparation 
96	for each individual.
97	In approaching strength training for the first time, it is important to remember that the increase in strength in 
98	relative newcomers is due primarily to a learning effect which is neuromuscular in nature. Such increases in 
99	strength related to performance factors such as the improvement in skill in executing a specific exercise can even 
100	take place within the first training session.  This type of improvement generally will be experienced with any 
101	exercise which is novel to the user. After that, strength changes occur in the following typical pattern (though the 
102	qualifying discussion in Section 1.12 should be noted):
103	96
104	
105	
106	===PAGE 108===
107	SUPERTRAINING
108	1. Increase in intermuscular coordination.  This functional improvement in the overall co-operation among 
109	different groups of muscles takes place over the first 2-3 weeks of training.
110	2. Increase in intramuscular coordination.  This next functional improvement, caused by enhanced cooperation 
111	between the fibres in a specific muscle group, continues for the following 4-6 weeks.
112	3. Increase in muscle hypertrophy. This first structural phase of significant increase in strength due to growth in 
113	muscle tissue becomes prominent during the next 6 to 12 weeks.
114	4. Stagnation. The rate of improvement for functional and structural reasons now decreases markedly. For 
115	continued progress, it now becomes necessary to determine whether the stagnation is due to neuromuscular 
116	or muscle growth factors and then modify the training programme accordingly. At this point, the knowledge 
117	of a highly skilled coach becomes necessary, especially as haphazard trial-and-error programmes initiated at 
118	the onset of the stagnation phase can diminish overall sports performance and lead to pain or injury.
119	Earlier sections of Chapter 1  (especially 1.6) and the immediately preceding section relate increases in strength to 
120	rw o broad physiological processes, namely hypertrophy and neural adaptation. More detailed analysis has 
121	associated more strength gain with hypertrophy of type II muscle fibres, with further information on changes in 
122	the different types of muscle fibre due to activation or inactivity appearing in Section 1.12.
123	Some caution is necessary before one overemphasizes the role of neural adaptation at the expense of other 
124	possible mechanisms of strength increase. Gains in peak force or joint torque after strength training have been 
125	documented in the absence of any changes in neural drive, as shown in studies which relied on training with 
126	electrical stimulation of the motor nerve or muscle, a process which ensured that the observed adaptations in peak 
127	torque were independent of neural, learning or motivational effects.
128	£ve/i though a relatively amateurish approach may produce strength increases during the first year of training,  
129	dtis may not be entirely beneficial to the athlete, because the improvements may not be sufficiently sports specific.  
130	From  the beginning, it is vital to identify exactly which strength-related qualities (such as speed-strength, skill- 
131	endurance or strength-endurance) need to be enhanced in a given individual executing a specific series of tasks in a 
132	particular sport. Both short- and long-term progress has to carefully planned if the path to Sports Mastery is to 
133	be efficient and largely injury-free.
134	2.1 Schemes for Perfecting Movements
135	Athletic performance may be described in terms of a complex interaction of many movements, so that the 
136	fundamental phenomenon underlying all sports tasks is movement. Sport then becomes a problem-solving activity  
137	in which movements are used to produce the necessary solutions.  These movements are controlled by the 
138	neuromuscular system, whose performance is the result of innate characteristics and the long-term acquisition of 
139	skills through training.
140	The perfecting of athletic movements during long-term training is realised primarily by enhancing the 
141	efficiency of the neuromuscular system to competently solve specific motor tasks. The ability to effectively use 
142	one's motor potential to achieve success is the essence of sports mastery. This ability is realised by means of a 
143	specific system of movements, the composition and organisation of which are determined by the type of athletic 
144	activity and the rules of competition. The sports training process as a whole is a phenomenon of exceptional 
145	complexity. In the context of this book, it is therefore appropriate to limit the study largely to those training 
146	schemes which relate most directly to muscular strength and the kinesiological organisation of movement in space 
147	and time, namely:
148	• Increasing the working effect of movements
149	• Perfecting the motor pattern of movements
150	• Perfecting the kinesiological pattern of movements.
151	2.1.1 Increasing the Working Effect of Movements

222	with concentration of force near the beginning of the movement. With this significant increase in maximum force, it 
223	shifts closer to the beginning of the movement and takes less time for its achievement (Fig 2.5).

249	2.1.2 Perfecting the Motor Pattern of Sports Movements
250	The effectiveness of movement is associated primarily with the appropriate use of the working mechanisms of the 
251	body. This produces mechanical energy for effective use in response to external conditions. Such working 
252	mechanisms are complcx and are largely inherited by each individual. Sports training adds nothing new to them, 
253	but only directs them to a high level of proficiency, improves their coordinated use and increases energy 
254	capabilities. The working mechanisms of the body include:

263	and functional characteristics of the body and facilitates optimal use of the working mechanisms under real 
264	sporting conditions. The body's mechanisms determine the form of the interaction during the execution of a given 
265	motor task and how systematic training uses them to produce efficient performance. It is useful to study the 
266	functional properties of the body's mechanisms and how they enhance specific performance at the following levels:
267	• The level of the kinematic pair (two actively combined adjacent links)
268	• The level of the kinematic chain (the sequential combination of several links)

358	The working movements of the body are produced by a system of links in a kinematic chain where the angles in 
359	each joint combination change simultaneously. The fundamental working functions of the kinematic chains in the 
360	motor apparatus consist of transforming rotational joint movements to linear movement (by lengthening or 
361	shortening the system's levers) or angular movement at the distal end of the system's links (relative to the proximal 
362	joint).
363	The working effect of the movements executed by the kinematic chain varies to a great extent, depending on 
364	specific conditions of the system at a given time (e.g. relative disposition of the links and the motor potential of 
365	given muscle groups). In addition, the working effect of exercises in kinematic chains is associated with larger 
366	qualitative and quantitative changes than in kinematic pairs. Perfecting of movement through the kinematic chain is 
367	secured by three basic factors:
368	• an increase in the working amplitude of the movement
369	• concentration of dynamic force at a certain part of it
370	• optimal interaction among the muscles involved.
371	An increase in the working amplitude is achieved by a large range of motion in the joint and by an increase in the 
372	elasticity and strength of the corresponding muscle groups and their associated connective tissues (Topolyan, 
373	1951; Ivanitsky, 1956; Donskoi, 1960). The amplitude of movement increases in two directions of the kinematic 
374	chain, namely the beginning and end of range. This is realised in the first case by an increase in muscular strength 
375	and the ability of the muscles to develop a powerful force during the movement, as well as an increase in the 
376	elasticity of the functional antagonists. The force produced shows two clear characteristics over the course of a 
377	movement:
378	1. A decrease in muscle tension at the end of the movement, especially with ballistic work (which is more 
379	pronounced for faster movement and smaller external resistance)
380	2. There is an increase and a concentration of working force at a certain part of the range of the movement.
381	The first characteristic is an obvious protective reflex as expressed by the inhibitory action of muscle antagonists, 
382	which is associated with the survival role of the motor system (Pierson, 1965). This mechanism does not change 
383	with growth in sports proficiency, which concerns the second characteristic, correlating directly with the process 
384	of producing a biomechanically appropriate movement, as discussed earlier.

STRENGTH TRAINING
Special Strength Training
Strength training has become vital for successful sports preparation. However, it is only of value if a specific 
methodology can be devised on the basis of scientific research, detailing the role and place of strength conditioning 
in the training process in the short and long term.
Regrettably, its historical links with physique training and the traditional view of muscle-bound gymnasium 
patrons have created the faulty impression that strength training retards athletic performance. Current emphasis 
on research into heart disease and cardiovascular physiology has served to consolidate this view by popularising 
the belief that fitness and cardiac health in general are well served by ’aerobic’ or cardiovascular exercise and 
endangered or minimally enhanced by training against resistance. The 'aerobics' community has confounded the 
picture further by empirically categorising many strength conditioning exercises as dangerous and generally 
regarding aerobic activity as superior to all other forms of exercise.
It often seems to be forgotten that fitness is a complex state determined by several interacting components 
(the fitness factors discussed in 1.14.3), each of which requires specialised training for optimal development. 
Strength processes play a particularly important role in controlling the stability and mobility of the body in sport.
Fortunately, a sizeable community of'strength scientists' has emerged to challenge the above preconceptions 
and examine the part played by strength and strength conditioning in human performance and injury rehabilitation. 
Some of their work is now revealing that muscle strength and endurance may play key roles in ensuring superior 
performance even during long duration events such as marathons. For instance, research into the biomechanics of 
the soft tissues has indicated that performance in distance running also may be enhanced by (Sifif, 1986):
• improving the ability of the SEC (series elastic component) of the muscle complex to store and release 
elastic energy
• modifying running technique to improve the ability of the athlete to utilise the stored elastic energy and to 
spare muscular energy.
As detailed in Chapter 1, the mechanical properties of connective tissues (such as elasticity, strength and damping 
ratio), as well as neuromuscular efficiency (discussed in later chapters), can be beneficially altered by using 
appropriate regimes of resistance and plyomctric training.
The striking success achieved by Russian and Eastern European coaches in applying specialised strength 
training in preparation for most sports has also stimulated the rest of the world to take this type of conditioning 
far more seriously. Considerable experience has now been gained in the use of special strength training to facilitate 
adequate analysis and identify some general principles. However, it has been insufficient to form a definitive 
methodological foundation for the special strength training of athletes. The role and place of special strength 
training can be established only through scientific research in two main directions:
• Further study of the principles governing the general  conditioning of the body to determine scientific means 
of achieving one's physical potential
• Intensive study of the principles determining the specific long-term sports training process.
Scicntific research in the first direction already has yielded a wealth of information, whereas serious work in the 
second direction has commenced only recently, so that its findings are still rather limited. Nevertheless, they 
enable one to formulate important principles concerning special strength training , where the latter term refers to 
the specialised application of strength training to sport. It is synonymous with sport specific strength training , 
and both expressions may be used interchangeably to distinguish it from general weight training or bodybuilding for 
aesthetic or casual fitness purposes.
At the outset, it must be emphasized that the phenomenon of strength should not be viewed simplistically in 
terms of the classical definition as 'the ability to produce force by action of the muscles'. Strength is highly context
2

dependent. This point will be stressed throughout this book, since strength can manifest itself in many forms, such 
as static strength, dynamic strength, strcngth-speed and strcngth-endurance. The accurate modelling of the 
strength and other fitness characteristics of a particular sport is what transforms general  strength training into 
special  strength training to produce consistent improvement in sports performance.
The Russian System of Classifying Athletes
Before going any further, it is relevant to remark on the use of the terms Sports Mastery  or Mastery in Sport. 
These terms have been used for many years in Russia and Eastern Europe to describe the process of reaching the 
highest possible level of sporting prowess.
They are also closely related to the categorisation scheme used to identify athletes of different qualification. 
In this scheme, competitors at the most basic level fall into Class III, athletes of intermediate standard into Class
II, and advanced athletes successively into Class I, Candidate for Master of Sport, Master of Sport, Candidate for 
International Master and International Master (or, Master of Sport, International Class). The last two categories 
refer to athletes such as world record holders, world champions and world champions of several years' standing. 
Specific norms are set for all individual and team sports, based on times, distances, scorcs, lifts, number of times of 
selection at a given team level or special achievements. The classification system does not rank beginners, since 
ranking is based on specific achievements.
It is one of the objectives of this book to present information which will assist the athlete to progress via the 
use of appropriate and effective strength training through all the stages of Mastery to the highest possible level 
dictated by his/her inherited potential.
It should be noted that the Russian system of classifying athletes begins not with formal competitions, but 
with the GTO (Readiness for Work and Defence) badge, which recognizes the minimum standards of physical 
fitness for anyone in the population. The GTO norms apply to children from about 10 years of age and progress 
into late adulthood (over 65 years of age). The GTO tests involve several sports and serve to identify levels of 
athletic prowess in the formative years. Those whose intention is to progress beyond the GTO IV, III, II and I 
badges have to pass more rigorous requirements to lead them through the various Classes of Mastery as detailed 
above. Before one reaches the adult classification system, there are also junior rankings (Class III up to Class I) foe 
athletes of up to 19 years.
The classification of athletes should not be regarded as a regimented system with strict application only in the 
Russian context, but a fundamental principle for the scientific preparation of athletes in all countries. Since 
athletes of different levels ofproficiency and training experience respond very differently to strength conditioning  
programmes , it is vital that competitors be periodically tested and graded to enable coaches to set up the most 
appropriate training regimen for each individual during a specific phase of development.
The Early Stages of Strength Training
A few remarks arc necessary about the early stages of strength training. Virtually any methods o f strength training  
will enhance the strength of a novice during the first few months , provided the intensity, in particular, is kept at a 
safe level. This is a major reason why it is misleading and counterproductive to apply the results obtained from 
scientific studies of less than at least six months' duration. It is also a major reason why relatively inexperienced 
coaches manage to have initial success with athletes and thereby continue to attract clients. Moreover, it has been 
discovered that each individual displays a different rate, degree and efficiency of responding to the same type,  
quality and quantity of physical training.  In other words, the identical training programme will have different 
effects on different people. The achievement of higher levels of mastery is a complex process which requires the 
careful application of the appropriate means and methods of training at the different stages of sports preparation 
for each individual.
In approaching strength training for the first time, it is important to remember that the increase in strength in 
relative newcomers is due primarily to a learning effect which is neuromuscular in nature. Such increases in 
strength related to performance factors such as the improvement in skill in executing a specific exercise can even 
take place within the first training session.  This type of improvement generally will be experienced with any 
exercise which is novel to the user. After that, strength changes occur in the following typical pattern (though the 
qualifying discussion in Section 1.12 should be noted):
96


===PAGE 108===
SUPERTRAINING
1. Increase in intermuscular coordination.  This functional improvement in the overall co-operation among 
different groups of muscles takes place over the first 2-3 weeks of training.
2. Increase in intramuscular coordination.  This next functional improvement, caused by enhanced cooperation 
between the fibres in a specific muscle group, continues for the following 4-6 weeks.
3. Increase in muscle hypertrophy. This first structural phase of significant increase in strength due to growth in 
muscle tissue becomes prominent during the next 6 to 12 weeks.
4. Stagnation. The rate of improvement for functional and structural reasons now decreases markedly. For 
continued progress, it now becomes necessary to determine whether the stagnation is due to neuromuscular 
or muscle growth factors and then modify the training programme accordingly. At this point, the knowledge 
of a highly skilled coach becomes necessary, especially as haphazard trial-and-error programmes initiated at 
the onset of the stagnation phase can diminish overall sports performance and lead to pain or injury.
Earlier sections of Chapter 1  (especially 1.6) and the immediately preceding section relate increases in strength to 
rw o broad physiological processes, namely hypertrophy and neural adaptation. More detailed analysis has 
associated more strength gain with hypertrophy of type II muscle fibres, with further information on changes in 
the different types of muscle fibre due to activation or inactivity appearing in Section 1.12.
Some caution is necessary before one overemphasizes the role of neural adaptation at the expense of other 
possible mechanisms of strength increase. Gains in peak force or joint torque after strength training have been 
documented in the absence of any changes in neural drive, as shown in studies which relied on training with 
electrical stimulation of the motor nerve or muscle, a process which ensured that the observed adaptations in peak 
torque were independent of neural, learning or motivational effects.
£ve/i though a relatively amateurish approach may produce strength increases during the first year of training,  
dtis may not be entirely beneficial to the athlete, because the improvements may not be sufficiently sports specific.  
From  the beginning, it is vital to identify exactly which strength-related qualities (such as speed-strength, skill- 
endurance or strength-endurance) need to be enhanced in a given individual executing a specific series of tasks in a 
particular sport. Both short- and long-term progress has to carefully planned if the path to Sports Mastery is to 
be efficient and largely injury-free.
2.1 Schemes for Perfecting Movements
Athletic performance may be described in terms of a complex interaction of many movements, so that the 
fundamental phenomenon underlying all sports tasks is movement. Sport then becomes a problem-solving activity  
in which movements are used to produce the necessary solutions.  These movements are controlled by the 
neuromuscular system, whose performance is the result of innate characteristics and the long-term acquisition of 
skills through training.
The perfecting of athletic movements during long-term training is realised primarily by enhancing the 
efficiency of the neuromuscular system to competently solve specific motor tasks. The ability to effectively use 
one's motor potential to achieve success is the essence of sports mastery. This ability is realised by means of a 
specific system of movements, the composition and organisation of which are determined by the type of athletic 
activity and the rules of competition. The sports training process as a whole is a phenomenon of exceptional 
complexity. In the context of this book, it is therefore appropriate to limit the study largely to those training 
schemes which relate most directly to muscular strength and the kinesiological organisation of movement in space 
and time, namely:
• Increasing the working effect of movements
• Perfecting the motor pattern of movements
• Perfecting the kinesiological pattern of movements.
2.1.1 Increasing the Working Effect of Movements
The writing effect of a movement is the result of interaction with objects in the environment, where speed and 
direction of movement depend upon the character of the force developed.
If the movement is to be analysed mathematically, then the force developed at any instant, F(t), may be 
depicted graphically (see Fig 2.1). In almost all athletic movements the beginning and end of the force curve lie on 
the horizontal axis, because the movement begins and ends with zero velocity. The working-effect of the effort is 
given by the area under the curve F(t) over the time interval t during which the weight W is overcome (the shaded

for definitions and derivations). An increase in the working-effect of the movement is achieved in principle bj 
increasing this area (i.e. its momentum). This, in brief, is one of the major goals for perfecting athletic movements 
Other major goals include increase in the maximum force (the peak of the F(t) graph), increase in the rate o f 
maximum force production (the upward slope of the F(t) graph in Fig 2.1), and production of maximum force t

The changc in the dynamics of an athletic movement, relative to its working amplitude, follows a regular sequence, 
namely (Fig 2.3b):
1. The movement initially displays a flattened distribution of force over much of the working range, which is
