1066	2.3.3 The Structure of Motor Abilities
1067	Very interesting data for understanding the structure of physical fitness were obtained in studies using factor 
1068	analysis in a complex of tests to assess the motor abilities of junior and senior athletes of different levels of 
1069	qualification in a variety of sports (Verkhoshansky, 1977). The experimental data of training for various lengths of 
1070	time of one group of athletes was analysed in specific cases. The factor structure of the athlete’s physical fitness 
1071	in a specific event, as well as the important changes in the structure connected with the growth in sports 
1072	proficiency, were examined.
1073	The number of factors increases with growth in proficiency and are distinguished from the avenge 
1074	characteristics by which motor abilities are assessed. This is expressed in the separation of one or two factors. For 
1075	example, the change in the structure of physical fitness of triple jumpers with growth in proficiency is connectcd 
1076	with subdivision of the first factor into separate components (a 30m sprint, a standing long jump and a standing 
1077	triple jump). Thus, if the factor composition of a junior jumper's physical fitness can be identified as special 
1078	sprint-jump fitness  and strength fitness , then a new factor must be added for more advanced jumpers, namely 
1079	explosive jumping strength  (the specific factor).
1080	The division of one relatively general, primary motor ability into two specific abilities is typical of the process 
1081	of forming the structure of the athlete's physical fitness (Verkhoshansky, 1977). For instance, practical 
1082	investigations have analysed the separation of the snatch and the clean-and-jcrk from squats and clean pulls as 
1083	performance indicators in weightlifting, the separation of absolute strength and relative strength as indices of 
1084	performance in volleyball, and the separation of the abilities to run with a running start and a regular start, as well 
1085	as running 30m and 100m from a regular start in sprinting and jumping.
1086	Factor analysis enables one to quantitatively assess the contribution of each factor in the general profile of 
1087	factors. This method was used to observe the changes in the relative importance of a specific factor with growth in 
1088	proficiency. It has been established that, concurrent with the change in the factor composition  (and consequently 
1089	the motor abilities which determine sporting success), there is a definite overestimation of their significance as 
1090	proficiency grows.
1091	One of them displays a greater significance, while another becomes less important. For instance, there is a 
1092	general tendency in speed-strength sports for muscular strength to decrease and the ability to produce explosive 
1093	force to increase (with the exception of weightlifters, because they experience a sharp increase in relative strength 
1094	with growth in proficiency).
1095	The fitness factor proportion of the individual motor abilities (such as absolute strength, starting strength and 
1096	acceleration strength) changes concurrently with growth in proficiency, i.e. the degree of correlation of proficiency 
1097	with the given factor. Two fundamental tendencies are observed here: an increase or a decrease in the correlation of 
1098	the individual fitness characteristics with the corresponding level of sports proficiency. This clearly corroborates 
1099	the above-mentioned decreasing role of absolute strength activities in enhancing specd-strength.
1100	Research also shows that the most important changes in the composition and structure of physical fitness 
1101	occur primarily during the beginning stage of training. At the high sports mastery level, significant changes in the 
1102	structure of physical fitness do not occur, thereby emphasizing the stability of the advanced neuromotor 
1103	programmes and the contributions by the individual fitness factors.
1104	2.3.4 General Concepts of the Structure of Physical Fitness
1105	In research and sports practice it is appropriate to divide motor abilities  into general and special abilities. 
1106	However, it should be emphasized that sporting performance is determined by a complex of motor abilities which 
1107	are qualitatively specific. They arc relatively independent in both their manifestation and development, and may 
1108	serve as determinants for a whole series of motor actions, all based on physiological processes.
1109	Taking into account the functional role of the determinant motor abilities, it is appropriate to divide them into 
1110	specific, non-specific  and levelling abilities.  The levelling abilities ensure the effective development of the key- 
1111	motor ability, which expresses the motor requirements of the specific sporting action. The levelling abilities, as 
1112	will be seen later, balance out and smooth the interaction between all other abilities.
1113	The role of specific abilities  is to secure the productivity of the key motor abilities. The non-specific ability 
1114	does not satisfy the particular motor requirements and therefore participates as an assisting factor 
1115	(Vcrkhoshansky, 1977). The role of the non-specific ability becomes apparent where the specific ability is 
1116	displayed under difficult conditions. For example, if speed of movement (the specific ability) is the primary

1125	The non-specific ability  can often negatively affect the key motor ability. For example, the excessive 
1126	development of absolute strength has a negative influence on speed.
1127	Levelling abilities play an important role in refining the key motor ability and in determining the structure of 
1128	general physical fitness. They smooth out clashes between the specific abilities and neutralise the influence of the 
1129	non-specific abilities if the latter act negatively against the specific abilities. Considering the diversity of motor 
1130	functions, where the formation of a whole series of non-specific motor abilities is possible, it should be recognized 
1131	that the levelling role of certain functions acquired by the body is vital for facilitating a high level of performance 
1132	under varying conditions.
1133	Finally, it should be noted that determinant motor abilities display their own complex combination of the 
1134	elementary motor abilities. Thus, with respect to physical fitness, the key determinant abilities and the elementary 
1135	abilities should be distinguished hierarchically (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Based on studies of the types of 
1136	connections between abilities (see 2.3.2), the principal structure of physical fitness may be represented as follows 
1137	(Fig 225):
1138	1. The key motor ability (KMA) is the result of the integrated development of a complex of determinants, 
1139	primarily the specific (SA) and non-specific (NSA) ability in each specific case.
1140	2. The levelling motor abilities  (LMA) participate in the process of motor integration as follows:
1141	• to smooth out the negative correlation between specific and non-specific abilities
1142	• to improve the connection between specific and non-specific abilities
1143	• to expand the functional range and the accommodative potential of the key abilities.
1144	3. Each of the determinant abilities is represented as a complex of elementary abilities (EA).
1145	Underlying the development of physical fitness is the organisational unity of the differentiation and integration of 
1146	the motor abilities. As a result, a new ability arises which is able to produce a strong working effect under a wide 
1147	range of conditions. This emerging ability displays a functional potential which is greater than the sum of the 
1148	properties of all the individual abilities.

1156	2. The specific motor ability (for example, explosive-strength) is, in general, largely an innate property of the

1164	Two hypotheses arise here: either the specific motor ability is functionally unrelated to the elementary motor 
1165	abilities or it is determined by a specific neuromotor structure which integrates part of the mechanisms of the 
1166	separate elementary forms of the motor abilities into a functional whole.
1167	It is difficult to accept the former hypothesis. Research and practical experience indicate that the formation 
1168	and development of specific motor abilities is not based upon the synthesis of the motor abilities developed 
1169	individually or the gradual transformation of some abilities into others. Instead, motor abilities retain their separate 
1170	characteristics and a specific neuromotor programme is established by rational training which integrates the 
1171	contributions of other motor abilities.

1176	specific neuromuscular structure  (SNS). The latter is the fundamental condition for developing explosive strength, 
1177	its specific neuromuscular structure displaying a particular functional form.

1179	physical fitness as a whole, and the mechanism of the key and specific motor abilities. In the former case, the 
1180	advantageous process of integration forms the foundation; in the latter case, the process of adaptive perfecting 
1181	already possesses a functional structure. The structure of physical fitness and the key motor ability is more 
1182	flexible and is formed on the basis of the wide diversity of the motor regimen. The specific motor abilities are m ore 
1183	conservative and their neuromuscular structure is developed only by a narrow range of means.

1185	complexity in the theory of sport. This complexity is due to the fact that the physiological processes of 
1186	integrating the motor abilities is as yet not sufficiently clear. Therefore, it is extremely important to determine the 
1187	statistical characteristics of the structure of physical fitness to serve as the basis for objectively assessing and 
1188	controlling factors which influence it.

These muscles act to oppose the force of gravity and the inertia of the body's mass obviously requires them to 
produce significant tension. On the other hand, the flexors of the hip have to overcome only the force of gravity 
and the inertial resistance of the mass of only one leg. Consequently, they require less emphasis on functional

Specialisation Processes
We should turn our attention to the fact that the starting-strength  and explosive strength  (see 2.2.1) increase 
slowly in the advanced sports mastery stage (Fig 2.22). As was shown previously, this is associated with a 
decrease in the effectiveness of the means of special strength training, which appears to be one of the reasons for 
the decrease in the growth of sporting performance. It can be assumed that the fundamental means of special- 
strength training in such a case is the sports exercise itself, executed at near-maximal intensity. Thus, the functional  
specialisation of the motor apparatus in the sports training process proceeds in a particular pattern, which may be 
expressed as follows (Verkhoshansky, 1977):
1. In the heterochronicity process, beginning with significant functional adaptation of certain muscle groups
2. In the different rates of functional adaptation of these muscle groups
3. In a specific sequence for developing the required motor abilities.
The fiinctional specialisation of the body in the sports training process occurs in two basic forms:
• Specialisation of the motor apparatus (certain parts of which display strong adaptation, i.e. principally 
those which handle the heavy fundamental work during the sports activity)
• Specialisation of the body as a whole and especially the isolation of the above-mentioned parts in 
developing those specific motor abilities which arc necessary for success in the given sports activity.
Thus, it is a matter of specialisation of the body by the physiological system on the one hand and by motor ability 
on the other. Specialisation by physiological system  is clearly local, restricted to specific muscle groups and their 
functional units. Specialisation by ability  is expressed in the development of such qualities of the body as a whole 
and chiefly the key working systems which primarily determine the level of its specific work capacity. As sports 
proficiency grows, the local character of the body's functional specialisation and the specificity of the motor 
abilities becomes more evident (see also 5.4.2, 5.4.3).
The pattern of long-term functional specialisation reflects essentially the natural course of adaptation (i.e. it is 
not really controllable, because its characteristics are largely unknown). It may be assumed that the time and other 
quantitative parameters of the stages and the trends in the functional specialisation of the body are not precisely 
definable at present. To enhance the effectiveness of long-term training, these parameters thus may be changed

2.3 Characteristics of Physical Fitness
Sports activity is characterised by the introduction of a physical regime to which the body is unaccustomed. The 
body attempts to accommodate to it with its entire complex of systems, including the central nervous, 
neuromuscular and muscular systems. Interaction between the various responses to these systems establishes the 
working efficiency of the body as a whole.
Thus, it is the form of the athlete’s physical fitness (i.e. the structural and functional adaptation of the body) 
that determines work capacity. The body’s work capacity acquires a certain specificity which depends on the type 
of sport. So, one can speak of the primary development of the ability to display qualities such as strength, speed 
and endurance, and call this key characteristic his motor function.
Each key function experiences a typical adaptation. It is largely inherent to any athlete of a given 
specialisation, although it can have an individual character in each case. Significantly distinct, individual differences 
can occur in the structure of strength fitness. Different athletes can obtain the same results using different 
contributions of work by the basic muscle groups, their different abilities to contract quickly, and their tendency 
to compensate for the functional lag of one muscle by more pronounced development of other muscles. Hence, the 
concept of the structure of strength fitness has great significance for organising strength training and especially for 
selecting effective means of developing muscular strength.
2.3.1 The Structure of Physical Fitness
The concept of the structure of physical qualities in general, has been formulated in a number of studies, but only 
as a statement of the problems involved (Zatsiorsky, 1961, 1965; Verkhoshansky, 1963, 1970, 1972). Until now a 
sufficiently thorough analysis has not been undertaken. At the same time, findings concerning the structure of 
physical fitness have been extensively covered in the literature, in particular concerning the interrelation between 
physical qualities (during their development); and the transfer of these qualities from one type of activity to 
another (Zimkin, 1965; Yakovlev et al, 1960; Zatsiorsky, 1965; Hebb 1949; Lindeburg, 1949; Nelson, 1957; 
Woodworth, 1958; Cratty, 1964). These studies have established that:
• The transference of physical qualities decreases with an increase in specific fitness (Zimkin, 1965; 
Zatsiorsky, 1965)
• The transference mechanism is to a great extent specific (Cumbeca et al 1957; Nelson 1957; Bachman, 1961;
Cratty, 1968; Lawther, 1968; Barrow, 1971)
• The interrelation between physical qualities can be positive, negative or neutral (Zimkin, 1956)
• Positive transference of certain qualities during the initial stages of training can lead later to negative 
transference (Korobkov, 1958).
It has often been claimed that complex training consisting of exercises which collectively involve speed, strength 
and endurance activities develops each of these qualities better than training each of them individually, even if the 
load is increased for the separate activities (Ozolin 1949, 1970). The validity of this assertion is examined later in 
this and later chapters.
The development of each quality positively influences the development of the others, and conversely, a lag in 
the development of one or more qualities limits the development of the others (Krestovnikov, 1951; Kaledin. 
1961). For example, the development of strength and speed develops the ability to display speed-strength 
(Zimkin, 1956; Kuznetsov, 1970).
Here the theoretical explanation is based on the mechanism of the conditioned reflex which underlies learned 
muscular activity. Training leads to the formation of an extensive background of temporary connections , which 
serves as a foundation on which various combinations of the motor activities can arise, depending upon the 
emphasis of training. It is assumed that, in the beginning, the training means should develop the motor qualities 
separately. They are later integrated on the basis of the sports movements which are structurally similar to them.
Recent developments have supplemented the 1930s' concept of the specificity of human motor abilities, based 
upon considerable research (Downey, 1923; Allport, 1933; McCloy, 1937; Vcrkhoshansky, 1970, 1972). This

emphasizes the highly complex relationships between motor abilities, the development of various means for the 
different kinds of muscle activity, and the consequent low degree of generality, high degree of specificity and poor 
transference from one type of activity to another.
The existence of general and specific abilities supports this concept. General abilities  form the basis for the 
ability to execute several different tasks, as they arc constant relative to any fluctuations of the conditions under 
which the task is executed. The general motor abilities provide the foundation for the execution of motor tasks and 
determine the relative stability of the neuromuscular system. They are regulated by heredity, physical structure 
and physiology.
Specific abilities reflect the functional specifics of performance in complex motor tasks, and are the chief 
results of motor experience gained by interaction with the environment. If general abilities facilitate the execution 
of several similar types of task, then specific abilities will be largely independent, enhancing only one specific 
activity. Attempts have been made to formulate theories explaining the physiology of specificity and the 
functional independence of different motor abilities with respect to neuromuscular coordination (Pitts, 1954; 
Henkey, 1960; Henkey & Whitlec 1960; Smith, 1962). However, these attempts remain largely speculative, since 
they are based on fairly rudimentary research.
Despite numerous studies, much is still unclear and contradictory regarding the nature of strength abilities. 
.Analysis of the literature identifies some of the conclusions on which specialists generally tend to agree 
(Verkhoshansky, 1970, 1972). In this respect, many articles assert that muscular strength developed by one 
means docs not have universal application, that there is no correlation between absolute muscular strength and 
speed of movement, that strength exercises decrease the speed of movement, that there is no relationship between 
static and dynamic strength, that there is no carry-over from isometric training to dynamic activity, and that 
dynamic strength relates more closely to motor performance than isometric strength.
However, it should be noted that such conclusions on the interrelation of motor abilities are often based on 
data obtained from subjects of low sports qualification and where the process of achieving sports mastery is not 
taken into consideration. It is therefore necessary to be very cautious about these conclusions and limit their 
applicability to those categories of athletes from which they were obtained and not to generalise prematurely.
The concept of the structure of an athlete's physical fitness (in particular, strength fitness) must be based on 
research and competitive performance. With respect to this, it is appropriate to distinguish between the 
composition and structure  of the athlete's physical fitness (Verkhoshansky, 1977). The composition  refers to the 
collection of all specific forms of the work capability which determine prowess in a given sport (e.g. strength, 
speed-strength, specd-endurance and other factors detailed in Section 1.15.4 and Table 8.1), whereas the structure  
refers to that complex interrelationship which functionally unites these independent motor abilities and determines 
the body's capability in that sport.
2.3.2 The Interrelation between Motor Abilities
Research enables us to recognise the following connections between motor abilities: general and partial, essential 
and non-essential, positive and negative, direct and indirect (Verkhoshansky, 1970, 1972 ; Scmyenov, 1971; 
Tatyan, 1974; Khodykin, 1976).
General and Partial Connections
A general connection is characterised by the interaction between any two motor abilities, including the influence of 
all other abilities, whereas a partial connection  involves only the indirect interaction between two abilities. 
Calculation of the general and partial correlations is used for quantitatively assessing these types of connections. 
Studies of the general and partial connections, using athletes of different specialisation and qualification have 
established that (Verkhoshansky, 1977):
1. Depending upon the abilities compared, the contribution of the partial connections can be lower (the most 
typical case) or higher than the contribution of the general connections.
2. The contribution of the partial connection between the same abilities in different sports is more stable than 
the contribution of the general connections.
Essential and Non-Essential Connections
These connections are characterised to a greater or lesser extent by the interaction of the motor abilities in sport. 
Research indicates that essential connections  (without which efficient sporting action is impossible) are more stable
117


===PAGE 129===
SUPERTRAINING
than non-essential connections  (spurious connections which may contribute to or detract from movemci 
efficiency) and can display a non-essential character which conceals the influence of the other abilities.
Positive and Negative Connections
These connections are also characterised by the relationship between motor abilities, where one of them may assir. 
(positive connection) or hinder (negative connection) the other. Research (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977) indicates that:
1. The positive connection  is the most characteristic of the complcx of motor abilities
2. The negative connection  appears primarily at the level of the partial connections
3. The positive connection, at the general correlation level, can bccome negative at the 
partial correlation level.
It should be noted that a negative connection has been repeatedly identified between such abilities as short and lon$ 
distance running, as well as absolute strength, speed of movement, and the ability to produce explosive fore* 
against a relatively small external resistance.
Direct and Indirect Connections
The direct connection  is characterised by a relationship between two abilities and can express any of the 
previously-described types of connections (Verkhoshansky, 1977). The indirect connection  is also a relation whet 
there is an essential, direct connection between two abilities. For example, there is no correlation between abilities 
A and B in Figure 2.23(a), but they are nevertheless connected through the third ability (C).
The latter connection is the most characteristic structure of physical fitness. For example, there is no direct 
significant connection between running speed and a sprinter’s absolute leg strength (it has already been mentioned 
that this connection is negative at the partial level). However, there is a close connection with jumping exercisci 
which are also rather closely connected with running speed. This emphasizes how important it is to have a clea* 
representation of the structure of an athlete's special strength fitness and use this to determine tasks and prescribe 
the means of special strength training.
Figure 2.23 Types of connections between motor abilities: theoretical model (a) and practical example (b) (Siff & Verkhoshanskv, 
1999).
The indirect connections  between motor abilities can be more complex. Thus, there is no direct, signifies 
connection (Fig 2.23b) between the height achieved in a vertical jump (h) and the absolute strength of the legs (So). 
However, absolute strength determines the magnitude of the maximal force of the take-off (Fmax) which, in turn, 
influences the magnitude of the impulse (F.t) of the push-off, and ultimately, the height of the jump.
The interdependence of the motor abilities changes both qualitatively and quantitatively with growth in spore 
proficiency. The most typical dynamics of the connections are changcs in the proportion of the above types o f 
connections between the separate abilities. In some cases, these involve a clear switch from one type of connection 
to another. Thus, while the partial connection  is preserved, the general connection  between individual abilities cat 
increase or decrease, because the non-essential connection  can acquire vital importance and vice-vera 
(Verkhoshansky, 1977). For example, triple jumpers lose some of their ability to execute the standing long jum: 
(or standing triple jump) and, conversely, increase their sprinting speeds (at 30m and 100m).
Positive and negative connections represent a special case. The changes in them are primarily one-sided witi 
growth in sports proficiency, i.e. from positive to negative (mainly at the partial correlation level), although* 
complete switch from one type to another is apparently impossible because of the influence of the third (levelling, 
ability.
118


===PAGE 130===
SUPERTRAINING
In the initial stages of training, the principle that 'all means are effective', is justified. However, as far as the 
development of physical fitness is concerned, the negative correlations between abilities appear more strongly than 
they should, but owing to the third ability, they level out. Levelling proceeds according to a principle of 
averaging, because of which the optimal correspondence between a number of abilities is achieved, facilitated by a 
decrease in both the direct and indirect connections (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
For example, the negative correlation between the 100m and the 1500m runs becomes even more apparent in 
decathlon athletes as the level of proficiency grows. However, because of the improvement in the ability to run 
400m, this correlation levels out by a decrease in the closeness of the connection between running the 400m and 
1500m, while it increases between the 100m and 400m run.
Direct and indirect connections between abilities display the smallest qualitative changes. They always 
characterise the structure of physical fitness, they are its specific properties, and changes are primarily 
quantitative. From the standpoint of quantitative changes, the connections between the individual abilities display 
two principal trends (Verkhoshansky, 1977):
• a decrease or increase in the closeness of the connection
• a linear or non-linear change of its indicators.
These trends may be illustrated concisely by means of a model of the correlational structure of the specific 
physical fitness of triple jumpers (Fig 2.24). This model analyses the connection between performance tests to 
determine the level of the jumper's sprinting, strength and jumping fitness.
The interconnecting lines between boxes in the diagram give the three coefficients of correlation (expressed as a 
percentage) relating to the performances of three groups of athletes of different levels of mastery in the triple 
jump. The first correlation coefficient refers to the jumping range of 13.50-14.49m for group 1, the second to the 
range of I4.50-I5.49m for group 2, and the last to the range of 15.50- 16.70m for group 3, respectively (there were 
40 men in each group).
Figure 2.24 Correlation flowchart of exercises for special physical preparedness of triple jumpers. The group of three numbers in each 
ease refers to the correlation coefficient expressed as a percentage for triple jumpers of increasing levels of sports mastery (Class 3,2, I, 
respectively). (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
119


===PAGE 131===
SUPERTRAINING
2.3.3 The Structure of Motor Abilities
Very interesting data for understanding the structure of physical fitness were obtained in studies using factor 
analysis in a complex of tests to assess the motor abilities of junior and senior athletes of different levels of 
qualification in a variety of sports (Verkhoshansky, 1977). The experimental data of training for various lengths of 
time of one group of athletes was analysed in specific cases. The factor structure of the athlete’s physical fitness 
in a specific event, as well as the important changes in the structure connected with the growth in sports 
proficiency, were examined.
The number of factors increases with growth in proficiency and are distinguished from the avenge 
characteristics by which motor abilities are assessed. This is expressed in the separation of one or two factors. For 
example, the change in the structure of physical fitness of triple jumpers with growth in proficiency is connectcd 
with subdivision of the first factor into separate components (a 30m sprint, a standing long jump and a standing 
triple jump). Thus, if the factor composition of a junior jumper's physical fitness can be identified as special 
sprint-jump fitness  and strength fitness , then a new factor must be added for more advanced jumpers, namely 
explosive jumping strength  (the specific factor).
The division of one relatively general, primary motor ability into two specific abilities is typical of the process 
of forming the structure of the athlete's physical fitness (Verkhoshansky, 1977). For instance, practical 
investigations have analysed the separation of the snatch and the clean-and-jcrk from squats and clean pulls as 
performance indicators in weightlifting, the separation of absolute strength and relative strength as indices of 
performance in volleyball, and the separation of the abilities to run with a running start and a regular start, as well 
as running 30m and 100m from a regular start in sprinting and jumping.
Factor analysis enables one to quantitatively assess the contribution of each factor in the general profile of 
factors. This method was used to observe the changes in the relative importance of a specific factor with growth in 
proficiency. It has been established that, concurrent with the change in the factor composition  (and consequently 
the motor abilities which determine sporting success), there is a definite overestimation of their significance as 
proficiency grows.
One of them displays a greater significance, while another becomes less important. For instance, there is a 
general tendency in speed-strength sports for muscular strength to decrease and the ability to produce explosive 
force to increase (with the exception of weightlifters, because they experience a sharp increase in relative strength 
with growth in proficiency).
The fitness factor proportion of the individual motor abilities (such as absolute strength, starting strength and 
acceleration strength) changes concurrently with growth in proficiency, i.e. the degree of correlation of proficiency 
with the given factor. Two fundamental tendencies are observed here: an increase or a decrease in the correlation of 
the individual fitness characteristics with the corresponding level of sports proficiency. This clearly corroborates 
the above-mentioned decreasing role of absolute strength activities in enhancing specd-strength.
Research also shows that the most important changes in the composition and structure of physical fitness 
occur primarily during the beginning stage of training. At the high sports mastery level, significant changes in the 
structure of physical fitness do not occur, thereby emphasizing the stability of the advanced neuromotor 
programmes and the contributions by the individual fitness factors.
2.3.4 General Concepts of the Structure of Physical Fitness
In research and sports practice it is appropriate to divide motor abilities  into general and special abilities. 
However, it should be emphasized that sporting performance is determined by a complex of motor abilities which 
are qualitatively specific. They arc relatively independent in both their manifestation and development, and may 
serve as determinants for a whole series of motor actions, all based on physiological processes.
Taking into account the functional role of the determinant motor abilities, it is appropriate to divide them into 
specific, non-specific  and levelling abilities.  The levelling abilities ensure the effective development of the key- 
motor ability, which expresses the motor requirements of the specific sporting action. The levelling abilities, as 
will be seen later, balance out and smooth the interaction between all other abilities.
The role of specific abilities  is to secure the productivity of the key motor abilities. The non-specific ability 
does not satisfy the particular motor requirements and therefore participates as an assisting factor 
(Vcrkhoshansky, 1977). The role of the non-specific ability becomes apparent where the specific ability is 
displayed under difficult conditions. For example, if speed of movement (the specific ability) is the primary
120


===PAGE 132===
SUPERTRAINING
requirement, but displaying it to a high level is difficult because of external resistance, then muscular strength (the 
non-specific ability) acts as an assisting factor. On the other hand, if the level of explosive strength decreases due 
to increasing fatigue, for example, then the required motor effect can be maintained by special endurance processes.
The non-specific ability  can often negatively affect the key motor ability. For example, the excessive 
development of absolute strength has a negative influence on speed.
Levelling abilities play an important role in refining the key motor ability and in determining the structure of 
general physical fitness. They smooth out clashes between the specific abilities and neutralise the influence of the 
non-specific abilities if the latter act negatively against the specific abilities. Considering the diversity of motor 
functions, where the formation of a whole series of non-specific motor abilities is possible, it should be recognized 
that the levelling role of certain functions acquired by the body is vital for facilitating a high level of performance 
under varying conditions.
Finally, it should be noted that determinant motor abilities display their own complex combination of the 
elementary motor abilities. Thus, with respect to physical fitness, the key determinant abilities and the elementary 
abilities should be distinguished hierarchically (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Based on studies of the types of 
connections between abilities (see 2.3.2), the principal structure of physical fitness may be represented as follows 
(Fig 225):
1. The key motor ability (KMA) is the result of the integrated development of a complex of determinants, 
primarily the specific (SA) and non-specific (NSA) ability in each specific case.
2. The levelling motor abilities  (LMA) participate in the process of motor integration as follows:
• to smooth out the negative correlation between specific and non-specific abilities
• to improve the connection between specific and non-specific abilities
• to expand the functional range and the accommodative potential of the key abilities.
3. Each of the determinant abilities is represented as a complex of elementary abilities (EA).
Underlying the development of physical fitness is the organisational unity of the differentiation and integration of 
the motor abilities. As a result, a new ability arises which is able to produce a strong working effect under a wide 
range of conditions. This emerging ability displays a functional potential which is greater than the sum of the 
properties of all the individual abilities.
Elementary Abilities
Figure 2.25 Model of the physical preparedness of an athlete (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
The development of the specific motor abilities is one of the conditions for establishing the structure of physical 
fitness. Before making assumptions about the mechanism of the specific motor abilities, it is necessary to consider 
the following points (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977):
1. The elementary motor abilities are functionally independent, are not transformed into the key abilities 
(specific) and preserve their own individuality with increase in fitness.
2. The specific motor ability (for example, explosive-strength) is, in general, largely an innate property of the 
motor apparatus.
121


===PAGE 133===
SUPERTRAINING
3. The specific motor ability is developed only by a particular motor regime.
Two hypotheses arise here: either the specific motor ability is functionally unrelated to the elementary motor 
abilities or it is determined by a specific neuromotor structure which integrates part of the mechanisms of the 
separate elementary forms of the motor abilities into a functional whole.
It is difficult to accept the former hypothesis. Research and practical experience indicate that the formation 
and development of specific motor abilities is not based upon the synthesis of the motor abilities developed 
individually or the gradual transformation of some abilities into others. Instead, motor abilities retain their separate 
characteristics and a specific neuromotor programme is established by rational training which integrates the 
contributions of other motor abilities.
This hypothesis can be expressed in the form of the principal scheme of the structure of explosive strength 
(Fig 2.26). This scheme emphasizes that the development of this ability, occurs under the control of a specific 
motor programme (SMP), which influences the components of explosive strength ( starting strength , absohst 
strength , acceleration-strength , and the reactive ability  to quickly produce unloaded movement, RA), and forms its 
specific neuromuscular structure  (SNS). The latter is the fundamental condition for developing explosive strength, 
its specific neuromuscular structure displaying a particular functional form.
It should be noted that there is a principal distinction between the mechanism which forms the structure of 
physical fitness as a whole, and the mechanism of the key and specific motor abilities. In the former case, the 
advantageous process of integration forms the foundation; in the latter case, the process of adaptive perfecting 
already possesses a functional structure. The structure of physical fitness and the key motor ability is more 
flexible and is formed on the basis of the wide diversity of the motor regimen. The specific motor abilities are m ore 
conservative and their neuromuscular structure is developed only by a narrow range of means.
It is necessary to control the formation of the structure of physical fitness, a problem which is of exceptional 
complexity in the theory of sport. This complexity is due to the fact that the physiological processes of 
integrating the motor abilities is as yet not sufficiently clear. Therefore, it is extremely important to determine the 
statistical characteristics of the structure of physical fitness to serve as the basis for objectively assessing and 
controlling factors which influence it.
Figure 2.26 Model of the specific motor structure of explosive strength. RA is the reactive ability to quickly produce unloaded 
movement. So is absolute strength and SNS is the Specific Neuromuscular Structure (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
So, the material examined in this chapter indicates that adaptation in sport seems to display various contradictions 
This is displayed by tendencies such as the integrative and separating character of the adaptive reaction, the 
generality and specificity of adaptation, and the unity of divergent and convergent processes during adaptation.
The tendencies mentioned express themselves in the local specialisation of the motor apparatus and the 
intensive development of specific motor abilities against the background of an increase in performance 
(Verkhoshansky, 1977). Functional adaptation begins with the body as a whole, then proceeds according to two 
interdependent paths, namely general adaptation  and specific adaptation.  At the same time adaptation develops 
independently because of the differentiating and separating character of physiological processes.
122


===PAGE 134===
SUPERTRAINING
Observations of adaptation in the body and its external relationships during long-term training show that 
measures of adaptive processes tend to correlate with sporting results (e.g. see 2.2.3). This assists in identifying 
the most typical dynamic and structural regularities of the sports training process (Verkhoshansky, 1966, 1970). 
The dynamics of the four fundamental components of sports proficiency relative to sports results (i.e. special 
work-capacity, ability to utilise motor potential, general fitness and specific fitness), may be expressed by the 
scheme illustrated in Figure 2.27.
Figure 2J7 Typical changes in the fundamental components of sports mastery over time. A is the athlete’s special work capacity, B is 
the athlete's ability to fully utilise his motor potential in sport. C refers to general fitness and D refers to special fitness. 
(Verkhoshansky, 1977).
Growth of special work-capacity chiefly determines sporting success; it improves steadily and correlates linearly 
with sports performance (A). Perfecting the ability to effectively utilise motor potential can be depicted as a 
monotonically growing curve, converging asymmetrically on the line describing the increase in the key motor 
ability (B). Improvement in the general work-capacity of the body can be expressed as a monotonically growing 
curve (C), and special fitness as a sharply rising and plateauing parabola (D).
The closeness of correlation between the various components of sports mastery differentiates, and determines 
to a large extent the motor specificity of the sporting movements (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Despite specific 
differences between some components, a certain regularity is observed in the dynamics of certain connections 
relative to improvement in performance. The principal changes in direction generally may be expressed graphically 
in the form of a vector correlation matrix  (Fig 2.28)
This schcme, which may be used to depict changes in the correlation between different components of sports 
mastery in a given sport, does not pretend to quantitatively express the dependencies precisely and it probably 
oversimplifies reality. However, it is sufficient to illustrate the characteristics of the dynamics of the fundamental 
components of the sports training process. It can serve as a starting point for long-term planning of training and 
as an ongoing indicator of the effects of an existing training programme, at least until there is a more rigorous 
mathematical analysis to yield more precise and reliable results.
It is relevant to make a few concluding remarks about sports technique which results from recognising certain 
regularities in the dynamics of the sports training process. The working-effect of a sporting movement is simply 
the result of the specific form of organisation and control of one's interaction with the environment. However, the 
fundamental concept of sports technique appears not merely as the organisation of the motor components of the 
sporting movement, but also as the athlete's ability to manage the external conditions competently and exploit the 
possibilities which they offer.
This ability is the result of many years of perfecting the motor functions and optimising use of all the body's 
systems. If this is so, then sports technique is the result of a certain form of the process developing over time, and 
consequently, as a specific scientific concept, it includes time coordinates. This determines an important principle, 
namely that sports technique is not a constant which can be achieved once, but is the result of continued progress 
from a lower to a higher level of perfection (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
This suggests that sports technique is widely understood in theory and practice as a means of solving motor 
problems. Strictly speaking, sports technique is a system of movement, representing not so much a means of 
solving motor problems, as the specific motor problem itself, which the athlete must solve every time he executes a 
sports exercise. Consequently, sports technique consists of the search for and the learning of relevant motor 
methods that provide the best way to use the one’s motor potential.
123


===PAGE 135===
SUPERTRAINING
Figure 2.28 Vector correlation matrix of changes in the closeness of the connections constituting the sports training process. The arrow 
depict the trend in the changes of the various connections (up refers to an increase, down to a decrease). (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
Therefore, the ability to achieve one's real potential in specific motor tasks by maintaining a particular system of 
movement is the essence of sporting proficiency. Continual improvement in this ability is fundamental to the 
training process and the degree to which motor potential is realised is the criterion of its effectiveness.
124

14	# Types of Maximal Strength (CFmax, TFmax, Fmm, Relative Strength)
15	
16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) separates "maximum strength" into a
17	ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
18	1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
19	competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
20	and absolute strength (Fmm, "maximum of all maxima," the involuntary ceiling reachable
21	only under electrical stimulation or a sudden reflex-recruited load, e.g. a sudden drop
22	or stretch reflex). Relative strength is strength per unit bodymass for a given lift.
23	Voluntary maxima also rank by contraction type, in order of magnitude: eccentric >
24	isometric > concentric. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1-2.)
25	
26	**Why it works** — Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
27	mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
28	structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further
29	than routine training effort does, which is why CFmax exceeds TFmax; involuntary or
30	reflex-driven recruitment removes still more of it, which is why Fmm exceeds CFmax.
31	
32	**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky states the competitive maximum, not the daily training
33	maximum, should set %-based intensity zones for higher-level athletes, because CFmax stays
34	comparatively stable while TFmax fluctuates day to day (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
35	**Inference:** this ladder is a useful lens for deciding which measured maximum should
36	anchor programmed intensity for a given athlete. **Eric's baseline:** the department
37	prefers VBT-estimated 1RM (Perch) over live 1RM attempts, estimating toward a target mean
38	velocity rather than forcing a true competitive-maximum attempt in the weight room
39	(`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`).
40	**Inference:** that preference is consistent with this framework's logic of anchoring
41	intensity to a stable maximum rather than a noisy daily one, though the baseline document
42	does not itself cite Zatsiorsky's TFmax/CFmax terminology.
43	
44	**When NOT to apply** — This is a terminology and reasoning framework, not a measured
45	protocol; Fmm requires electrical stimulation or reflex loading, which Verkhoshansky
46	himself calls impractical (PDF p. 12, printed p. 1). **Inference:** none of these four
47	maxima are named as routinely and directly measured in Baylor's own documented protocols
48	(`method-baseline.md`), so this should be treated as a mental model for why training-day
49	and competition-day 1RMs diverge, not as a set of numbers to test for. Verkhoshansky states
50	the eccentric > isometric > concentric ordering is a general tendency, not a fixed ratio,
51	varying by joint angle, velocity, and muscle group (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2, cross-referenced
52	to 1.2).
53	
54	**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete's best training-day squat (TFmax) is consistently lower than
55	what they hit in a max-out competition or meet (CFmax); programming off the meet number
56	rather than a re-tested gym max avoids under-loading the athlete for weeks after a strong
57	competitive performance.
58	
59	**Related** — [[claim--voluntary-involuntary-strength-reserve-magnitudes]] (the numeric
60	gaps between these maxima); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
61	(a practical field proxy for the same voluntary/involuntary gap).

# Types of Maximal Strength (CFmax, TFmax, Fmm, Relative Strength)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) separates "maximum strength" into a
ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
and absolute strength (Fmm, "maximum of all maxima," the involuntary ceiling reachable
only under electrical stimulation or a sudden reflex-recruited load, e.g. a sudden drop
or stretch reflex). Relative strength is strength per unit bodymass for a given lift.
Voluntary maxima also rank by contraction type, in order of magnitude: eccentric >
isometric > concentric. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1-2.)

**Why it works** — Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further
than routine training effort does, which is why CFmax exceeds TFmax; involuntary or
reflex-driven recruitment removes still more of it, which is why Fmm exceeds CFmax.

**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky states the competitive maximum, not the daily training
maximum, should set %-based intensity zones for higher-level athletes, because CFmax stays
comparatively stable while TFmax fluctuates day to day (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
**Inference:** this ladder is a useful lens for deciding which measured maximum should
anchor programmed intensity for a given athlete. **Eric's baseline:** the department
prefers VBT-estimated 1RM (Perch) over live 1RM attempts, estimating toward a target mean
velocity rather than forcing a true competitive-maximum attempt in the weight room
(`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`).
**Inference:** that preference is consistent with this framework's logic of anchoring
intensity to a stable maximum rather than a noisy daily one, though the baseline document
does not itself cite Zatsiorsky's TFmax/CFmax terminology.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a terminology and reasoning framework, not a measured
protocol; Fmm requires electrical stimulation or reflex loading, which Verkhoshansky
himself calls impractical (PDF p. 12, printed p. 1). **Inference:** none of these four
maxima are named as routinely and directly measured in Baylor's own documented protocols
(`method-baseline.md`), so this should be treated as a mental model for why training-day
and competition-day 1RMs diverge, not as a set of numbers to test for. Verkhoshansky states
the eccentric > isometric > concentric ordering is a general tendency, not a fixed ratio,
varying by joint angle, velocity, and muscle group (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2, cross-referenced
to 1.2).

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete's best training-day squat (TFmax) is consistently lower than
what they hit in a max-out competition or meet (CFmax); programming off the meet number
rather than a re-tested gym max avoids under-loading the athlete for weeks after a strong
competitive performance.

**Related** — [[claim--voluntary-involuntary-strength-reserve-magnitudes]] (the numeric
gaps between these maxima); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
(a practical field proxy for the same voluntary/involuntary gap).

14	# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops
15	
16	**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), Verkhoshansky states biochemical adaptation to
17	training follows a definite sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first, oxidative ATP
18	resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle protein (myosin)
19	and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase; only after that
20	does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining or detraining, these
21	adaptations are lost in the reverse order they were gained. The longer the training period,
22	the more thorough the adaptation and the longer those biochemical changes persist after
23	training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels). This gain/loss asymmetry across
24	different systems is termed heterochronic (different tissues and processes change on
25	different timelines). Overtraining specifically shows a distinct pattern: reduced
26	glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/glycogen, blood plasma
27	dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to disrupted acid-base
28	balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)
29	
30	**Why it works** — Different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity, structural protein
31	synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular mechanisms with
32	different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts, then de-adapts"
33	model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while others are gained
34	late and lost early.
35	
36	**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's own conditioning material states
37	that traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining, while traits
38	hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest, and uses this ordering to sequence how
39	often each quality needs re-exposure (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
40	systems," citing `class-4-2026.md p.47`). **Inference:** this converges directionally with
41	Platonov's heterochronic principle (different systems have different adaptation/de-
42	adaptation timelines) but the two are not a stated one-to-one match — the baseline's
43	build-easy/lose-fast claim is about energy-system categories (aerobic vs. alactic), while
44	Platonov's sequence is about biochemical sub-processes within training generally (oxidative
45	capacity, structural protein, glycolysis, CP). Treat them as parallel instances of the same
46	underlying heterochronicity concept, not as the same specific claim restated.
47	
48	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific ordering (oxidative/glycogen, then
49	structural protein/glycolysis, then CP) is cited to one secondary source (Platonov, 1988)
50	without the underlying primary data described in this text; do not treat this exact
51	four-stage sequence as a settled, universally-timed protocol for monitoring detraining. Use
52	it as a general principle (adaptation and loss are not uniform across systems) rather than
53	a specific testing checklist.
54	
55	**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete returning from a multi-week layoff might show
56	CP-system/power qualities holding up relatively better than the earlier-gained oxidative
57	and glycogen-storage qualities, or vice versa, depending on the specific loss sequence;
58	either way, "detraining" is not a single uniform decline and re-testing across qualities
59	(not just one) gives a more accurate readiness picture.

14	# Strength Training Adapts Along (at Least) Ten Independent, Narrow Dimensions
15	
16	**What it is** — Strength gains transfer narrowly, not generally, across at least ten
17	independent dimensions: type of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region/range of
18	movement, velocity of movement, force of contraction, muscle fibre recruitment,
19	metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility, and fatigue. Training that improves one
20	dimension often produces little or no improvement on the others, even when the same
21	muscle groups are involved. Specificity is explicitly distinguished from simulation:
22	mimicking a sport movement with added resistance is not the same as training the specific
23	factors above, and can actually distort the neuromuscular programming needed for the real
24	skill because of changes in center of gravity, moment of inertia, and mechanical
25	stiffness introduced by the resistance. (PDF pp. 38-39, printed pp. 27-28.)
26	
27	**Why it works** — Strength adaptation is produced and expressed by the nervous and
28	muscular systems together (see
29	[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]); the specific
30	demands (velocity, joint angle, contraction type, metabolic pathway) shape which
31	recruitment patterns, fibre types, and biochemical pathways are trained, so a change in
32	any one of those parameters can produce a materially different, largely non-transferable
33	adaptation. This is one of the more broadly replicated findings in strength and
34	conditioning research, independent of this text.
35	
36	**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a master reasoning check before assuming an
37	exercise "transfers" to a sport skill: ask which of the ten dimensions the exercise
38	actually matches, not just whether it uses similar muscles. **Eric's baseline:** the
39	Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of
40	movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production,
41	and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise transfers, and
42	is taught in HHPR 5355 (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
43	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14`, `week1-lecture.md p.34`). **Inference:**
44	Dynamic Correspondence (this book's Ch4.3, not yet ingested) is plausibly the applied
45	extension of this same ten-dimension specificity logic to exercise selection, though this
46	chapter does not itself state that link.
47	
48	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't use "specificity" as an argument against any
49	general preparation work; this book's own 1.1 material and this library's Bompa
50	multilateral/LTAD entries support building a general base before narrowing to sport-specific
51	work. This principle governs which dimensions transfer, not whether general work has value
52	at an earlier training age; that distinction is this entry's own reading, not stated as
53	such in this passage of the text.
54	
55	**Example** — **Inference:** Heavy squat strength does not automatically transfer to high-velocity sprint
56	force production (different point on the velocity dimension) even though both use similar
57	musculature; each needs its own specific training exposure.

# The Force-Time Curve Changes a Specific Way With Long-Term Training, and the Pattern Differs by Movement Type

**What it is** — As sports proficiency grows, an athlete's force-time curve F(t) and
force-displacement curve F(s) change in a consistent overall pattern: the time to reach
maximal force decreases, maximal force increases, the point of maximal effort moves closer
to the start of muscle tension, and the total duration of the effort decreases. Verkhoshansky
cites his own longitudinal data (a leg-extension task, before and after 6 months of
training) and several other Soviet studies of athletes at different qualification levels as
support (PDF pp. 118-119, printed pp. 97-98, Figs 2.1-2.3). He then describes four distinct
sub-patterns by movement type, all sharing that same general trend but differing in where
force concentrates over the range of motion:
- **Large-resistance movements** (gymnastics, wrestling, weightlifting): perfecting is
  realised mainly by increasing maximum force with some decrease in time to produce it.
- **Ballistic/small-resistance movements** (fencing, some throwing): force concentrates near
  the *beginning* of the movement, shifting earlier and taking less time as mastery grows.
- **Stretch-shortening movements** (jumping, figure skating, acrobatics): perfecting comes
  from improving the muscles' ability to generate force during the eccentric-to-concentric
  transition, which shortens the working amplitude (a smaller joint-flexion angle) as
  mastery grows.
- **Cyclic movements** (running, swimming, rowing): perfecting comes from producing maximum
  force faster out of a deep, rapid relaxation phase, with a relatively longer relaxation
  phase and a shorter absolute cycle duration.
(PDF pp. 119-121, printed pp. 98-100, Figs 2.4-2.7.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no single unified mechanism for why the curve
reshapes this way across all four movement types; he attributes it to the general
perfecting of neuromuscular coordination and the kinesiological pattern (see
[[framework--kinesiological-pattern-and-strength-field-components]]) rather than a single
physiological cause. **Inference:** the shared trend (faster force onset, higher peak,
shorter total duration) is consistent with well-replicated modern findings that RFD and
neural drive improve with resistance training independent of large hypertrophy changes,
which would explain the timing shift; the movement-specific location of where force
concentrates is better explained by task constraints (available time, external resistance,
and whether the movement uses a stretch-shortening cycle) shaping which part of the range
the nervous system learns to emphasize.

**When to apply** — Use this as a framework for reading a force-time curve (e.g. a CMJ or
squat-jump trace from ForceDecks) against the athlete's event demands: a lineman's drive
block or a powerlifting-style movement should be read against the "large-resistance"
pattern (rising peak force, tightening time-to-peak), while a jump or plant-and-cut action
should be read against the "stretch-shortening" pattern (a shortening, more efficient
amortization). **Eric's baseline:** the department already runs the full ForceDecks CMJ
family and reports driver metrics like braking/propulsive force and phase durations under
the ODSF framework (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`, `hd-odsf-metrics.md`). **Inference:** this framework
gives a training-adaptation lens for interpreting a trend in those phase-duration and
force metrics over a training block (e.g. a shortening amortization phase across a training
cycle) as a sign of the expected stretch-shortening-cycle adaptation, not just a data point.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive pattern of *change over
training time*, not a same-day diagnostic; a single force-time trace cannot show whether an
athlete's curve is "improving" without a comparable baseline trace from earlier in that
athlete's training history. The four movement-type categories are the book's own taxonomy,
built from a handful of Soviet studies (Verkhoshansky 1961, 1963; Papysheva 1966; Gomberazde
1970; Semyenov 1970; Tatyan 1974) rather than a broad modern meta-analysis, so treat the
specific shapes (not just the general trend) as `supported`, not `proven`. Do not assume
every sport fits cleanly into one category; many football positions blend large-resistance
demands (line play) with stretch-shortening and cyclic demands (change of direction,
sprinting) within the same athlete.

**Example** — A running back's CMJ force-time trace, tracked across an off-season block,
would be expected (per this framework) to show a shortening, more front-loaded braking
phase and a higher, earlier propulsive peak as reactive strength improves, distinct from an
offensive lineman whose relevant curve (a drive-block or isometric mid-thigh pull trace)
would be expected to show a rising peak force with a flatter, less time-compressed profile.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Chapter 1),
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (Chapter 1, the SEC mechanism behind
the stretch-shortening pattern here).

pair level, force output depends heavily on joint angle (maximum isometric force occurs at
a specific angle per joint, e.g. approximately 90 degrees for elbow flexion, 120 degrees for
elbow extension, 60-70 degrees for shoulder extension, 60 degrees for knee extension); at
the chain level, perfecting comes from increasing working amplitude, concentrating dynamic
force at a specific part of the range, and optimizing the sequencing of muscle
participation (proximal muscles initiate, distal links follow, with fixation at proximal
joints to create a stable base); at the system level, the same chain-level mechanisms
extend across a larger number of interacting muscle groups, chiefly the legs and torso
followed by the shoulder girdle.

changes muscle length and the angle of pull, which changes torque about the joint, which is

energy at the bottom of a vertical jump). **Inference:** no single unifying mechanism is

level of exercise) actually matches a sport skill: an isolated single-joint exercise trains
at the kinematic-pair level and, per this text, transfers narrowly; a compound lift like a
clean or a squat trains at the chain level; a sprint start or a blocking movement operates
at the whole-system level and cannot be fully represented by any single-joint or even

# Training at a Joint's Longest-Muscle-Length Angle Transfers More Evenly; Training at a Shortened Angle Gains More but Transfers Less

**What it is** — Citing Zatsiorsky & Raitsin (1974) and Raitsin & Sarsania (1975),
Verkhoshansky states that where in the range of motion an athlete trains a single-joint
movement changes how that strength gain transfers to other joint angles. If maximum
muscular force is trained at the angle corresponding to the muscle's greatest length (the
smallest degree of flexion for active flexion work, or the least extension for extension
work), the resulting strength increase transfers relatively uniformly to other joint
angles. If maximum force is instead trained with the joint significantly flexed and the
muscle in a shortened state, the resulting strength increase at that specific angle is
larger, but transfers comparatively poorly to other joint angles, with transfer falling off
further the farther the target angle is from the trained one. (PDF pp. 123-124, printed pp.
102-103.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no cellular mechanism in this passage; he treats it as
an established empirical regularity from isometric training-at-a-single-angle studies. **Inference:**
a plausible mechanism (not stated in this passage) is that training at a lengthened position
recruits a joint-angle range closer to what most functional tasks pass through on the way to
lockout, so gains generalize across the arc, whereas training in a fully shortened position
trains a narrow, less commonly used part of the strength curve, producing a large but
narrowly-tuned adaptation (consistent with the general specificity principle in
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when deciding where in the range to bias a
strength exercise for an athlete who needs broad strength across a joint's full range (most
field-sport athletes) versus one who needs a large gain at one specific, narrow joint angle
that matches a single sport position (e.g. a very specific start-position strength need).
Favor training through, or anchored near, the lengthened position when general transfer
across a range of joint angles is the goal.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from isometric single-joint training studies from the
1970s (Zatsiorsky & Raitsin, 1974; Raitsin & Sarsania, 1975), not from dynamic, multi-joint,
or modern resistance-training methodology; **Inference:** do not assume this angle-specific
transfer pattern applies identically to dynamic full-range lifts (e.g. a full back squat),
where the muscle passes through many angles within a single repetition rather than training
isometrically at one fixed angle. The text also states the *shape* of the force-angle curve
itself does not change fundamentally with training, only the amount transferred across it,
so this claim is about magnitude of transfer, not about reshaping the underlying joint-angle
strength curve.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete doing isometric mid-thigh-pull-style training near
a lengthened hip/knee position would be expected, per this claim, to show more even carryover
to strength expressed at other joint angles than an athlete who only trains isometric holds
in a deep, shortened flexed position, who would gain more at that specific angle but less
elsewhere.

**Related** — [[framework--kinematic-pair-chain-system-movement-analysis-levels]],
[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]],
[[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]] (Chapter 1).

90 degrees as isometric testing suggests, but nearer full flexion, and evoking the myotatic
stretch reflex with a ballistic start near full extension produces yet another profile. The

# The "Strength Field": Five Force Components That Make Up Every Sports Movement, and the "Kinesiological Pattern" That Organizes Them

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky defines the **strength field** of a motor task as the sum of
all external and internal forces acting on the body while it executes that task, made up of
five components: (1) the active driving force from muscular contraction, (2) the reactive
force arising from the active muscles' interaction with the environment, (3) force stored as
elastic energy in the muscle complex during a preparatory (stretching) phase, (4) the force
of inertia of the body or its links, and (5) the weight of the body or its links. The
**kinesiological pattern** is the specific, hierarchical organization of voluntary and
reflexive elements within that strength field for a given sport skill; he uses this term
rather than "biomechanical pattern" deliberately, to signal that a motor action is not just
physics acting on a body but an active process shaped by psychological and physiological
factors together. As sports mastery grows, the kinesiological pattern moves from weak,
irregularly distributed force elements (Fig 2.12a) to a tightly organized, hierarchical
system with dominant "key" elements and subordinate ones (Fig 2.12b), reproducible with less
variation and over a shorter time. Acyclic exercises (a single explosive effort) are trained
mainly by forming and refining this pattern; cyclic exercises (running, swimming) develop the
pattern faster and more simply, so training there centers more on perfecting involuntary,
repetitive contributions. (PDF pp. 133-137, printed pp. 106-110, sourced to Verkhoshansky
1958, 1963, 1966, 1968, 1977.)

**Why it works** — The author does not give a single causal mechanism for why the
kinesiological pattern tightens with mastery; he frames it as an emergent property of
repeated adaptation, where the correlation between elements strengthens (a change in one
element is reflected in others, even those separated in space and time) and a hierarchy of
dominant/subordinate elements forms. **Inference:** this is consistent with motor-learning
concepts of coordinative structure formation (movement components becoming functionally
linked with practice), though the text does not cite motor-learning literature directly to
support that link.

**When to apply** — Use the five-component strength field as a checklist when analyzing
why a movement produces the force output it does, and to decide which special-strength
training means (see later chapters) should target which component: e.g. a movement that
depends heavily on stored elastic energy (component 3) calls for plyometric or reactive
methods, while one that depends mainly on the active driving force (component 1) calls for
more conventional strength methods. **Inference:** this is a useful diagnostic lens for
reading a force-plate trace or coaching cue: ask which of the five components is limiting a
given athlete's output in a given task, rather than defaulting to "get stronger" as the only
lever.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this framework is a conceptual organizing scheme, not
a measured or validated model; the text gives no method for quantifying each of the five
components separately in a real sports movement, so treat it as a way to structure thinking
about a movement's force sources, not as a set of directly testable variables. Do not confuse
"kinesiological pattern" with a simple biomechanical description of joint angles over time;
the term is explicitly meant to include the reflexive and adaptive character of the pattern,
which a purely kinematic (position/angle) analysis would miss.

**Example** — In a vertical jump, the strength field includes the active quadriceps/glute
drive (component 1), ground reaction force (component 2), elastic energy stored during the
countermovement dip (component 3), the inertia of the body's mass being redirected (component
4), and body weight (component 5); an athlete with a weak amortization phase is likely
under-using component 3, which a purely strength-focused (component 1) training emphasis
would not fix.

**Related** — [[framework--kinematic-pair-chain-system-movement-analysis-levels]],
[[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (Chapter 1),
[[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]] (Chapter 1).

# Whether a Sport Rewards Fast Force (RFD) or Total Force/Momentum Should Decide Whether You Train Max Strength or Explosive Strength

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky illustrates with a thought experiment (Fig 2.14-2.15): two
athletes perform a maximal single repetition of the same exercise as fast as possible, then
hold the load until fatigue. Athlete B produces a greater maximum force and sustains force
longer overall (greater area under the curve, i.e. greater momentum and muscle endurance).
Athlete A, however, produces *more* force than B at any early instant before a crossover time
T2 (i.e. a faster Rate of Force Development). If the sport requires rapid RFD (jumping,
striking, throwing sports such as basketball, martial arts, track and field), athlete A has
the advantage, and training aimed at increasing athlete B's maximal strength or muscle bulk
would be "misdirected" for that goal; that athlete instead needs explosive-strength (RFD)
training. If the sport instead requires high maximal force or momentum regardless of timing
(wrestling, powerlifting, rugby scrumming, judo), athlete B has the advantage, and athlete A
will not improve without training to increase maximal strength. (PDF pp. 130-132, printed pp.
109-110.)

**Why it works** — Maximal force and Rate of Force Development are separable qualities
because most sporting actions occur inside a limited time window; an athlete can be strong
