# Three Levels for Analyzing a Movement: Kinematic Pair, Kinematic Chain, Kinematic System

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky organizes movement analysis into three nested levels of
increasing complexity (PDF pp. 121-125, printed pp. 100-104): the **kinematic pair** (a
single joint, or two actively combined adjacent links, e.g. isolated knee extension), the
**kinematic chain** (a sequential combination of several links working together, e.g. hip +
knee + ankle in a jump take-off), and the **kinematic system** (the combination of several
kinematic chains into one whole-body action, e.g. legs, torso, and shoulder girdle acting
together). Perfecting movement at each level has its own characteristic mechanism: at the
pair level, force output depends heavily on joint angle (maximum isometric force occurs at
a specific angle per joint, e.g. approximately 90 degrees for elbow flexion, 120 degrees for
elbow extension, 60-70 degrees for shoulder extension, 60 degrees for knee extension); at
the chain level, perfecting comes from increasing working amplitude, concentrating dynamic
force at a specific part of the range, and optimizing the sequencing of muscle
participation (proximal muscles initiate, distal links follow, with fixation at proximal
joints to create a stable base); at the system level, the same chain-level mechanisms
extend across a larger number of interacting muscle groups, chiefly the legs and torso
followed by the shoulder girdle.

**Why it works** — The author gives a partial mechanism at the pair level: joint angle
changes muscle length and the angle of pull, which changes torque about the joint, which is
why force-angle curves are joint-specific (Figs 2.8-2.11, citing Zatsiorsky 1966;
Verkhoshansky 1970). At the chain level, he attributes the sequencing pattern to how the
body distributes work so that each joint operates near its own angle of maximum strength
where possible, with the deficit made up by stored elastic energy from a preceding
countermovement or amortization phase (e.g. the knee-extension assist from stored elastic
energy at the bottom of a vertical jump). **Inference:** no single unifying mechanism is
given for why analysis "levels" (pair vs. chain vs. system) should matter to a coach beyond
organizing the complexity of the problem; this is presented as a taxonomy for structuring
analysis, not itself a tested causal model.

**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy to decide what level of analysis (and therefore what
level of exercise) actually matches a sport skill: an isolated single-joint exercise trains
at the kinematic-pair level and, per this text, transfers narrowly; a compound lift like a
clean or a squat trains at the chain level; a sprint start or a blocking movement operates
at the whole-system level and cannot be fully represented by any single-joint or even
single-chain exercise. **Eric's baseline:** exercise selection is already organized on a
general-to-specific spectrum (general preparation, specific preparation, specific
development, competitive exercises, per Bondarchuk) and weighted toward high
motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements with single-joint work kept to a small share
of volume (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13`, `week1-lecture.md p.31`). **Inference:** this
framework gives the underlying biomechanical reasoning for that weighting: whole-system,
chain-level exercises train the sequencing and joint-angle coordination that a sport skill
actually needs, while isolated single-joint work only trains the narrower kinematic-pair
level.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive analysis taxonomy, not a
prescription that single-joint (kinematic-pair) work has no value; the book's own material
elsewhere treats isolated joint-angle training as informative for identifying weak links
(see [[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]). Do
not use "kinematic system" language as a stand-in for real coaching observation: the text
itself notes the mechanisms at the chain and system levels are "the same," differing only in
the number of interacting muscle groups, so system-level claims should be checked against
the same chain-level evidence rather than treated as a separate, more rigorously established
category.

**Example** — A leg-extension machine trains at the kinematic-pair level (single knee
joint, fixed angle range); a back squat trains at the kinematic-chain level (hip, knee, and
ankle sequenced together); a football offensive lineman's drive block trains at the
kinematic-system level (legs, torso, and arms coordinated as one unit against an external
opponent), and no amount of leg-extension or even squat work alone can be assumed to fully
transfer to that system-level skill.

**Related** — [[framework--kinesiological-pattern-and-strength-field-components]],
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1),
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]].

# The "Strength Field": Five Force Components That Make Up Every Sports Movement, and the "Kinesiological Pattern" That Organizes Them

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky defines the **strength field** of a motor task as the sum of
all external and internal forces acting on the body while it executes that task, made up of
five components: (1) the active driving force from muscular contraction, (2) the reactive
force arising from the active muscles' interaction with the environment, (3) force stored as
elastic energy in the muscle complex during a preparatory (stretching) phase, (4) the force
of inertia of the body or its links, and (5) the weight of the body or its links. The
**kinesiological pattern** is the specific, hierarchical organization of voluntary and
reflexive elements within that strength field for a given sport skill; he uses this term
rather than "biomechanical pattern" deliberately, to signal that a motor action is not just
physics acting on a body but an active process shaped by psychological and physiological
factors together. As sports mastery grows, the kinesiological pattern moves from weak,
irregularly distributed force elements (Fig 2.12a) to a tightly organized, hierarchical
system with dominant "key" elements and subordinate ones (Fig 2.12b), reproducible with less
variation and over a shorter time. Acyclic exercises (a single explosive effort) are trained
mainly by forming and refining this pattern; cyclic exercises (running, swimming) develop the
pattern faster and more simply, so training there centers more on perfecting involuntary,
repetitive contributions. (PDF pp. 133-137, printed pp. 106-110, sourced to Verkhoshansky
1958, 1963, 1966, 1968, 1977.)

**Why it works** — The author does not give a single causal mechanism for why the
kinesiological pattern tightens with mastery; he frames it as an emergent property of
repeated adaptation, where the correlation between elements strengthens (a change in one
element is reflected in others, even those separated in space and time) and a hierarchy of
dominant/subordinate elements forms. **Inference:** this is consistent with motor-learning
concepts of coordinative structure formation (movement components becoming functionally
linked with practice), though the text does not cite motor-learning literature directly to
support that link.

**When to apply** — Use the five-component strength field as a checklist when analyzing
why a movement produces the force output it does, and to decide which special-strength
training means (see later chapters) should target which component: e.g. a movement that
depends heavily on stored elastic energy (component 3) calls for plyometric or reactive
methods, while one that depends mainly on the active driving force (component 1) calls for
more conventional strength methods. **Inference:** this is a useful diagnostic lens for
reading a force-plate trace or coaching cue: ask which of the five components is limiting a
given athlete's output in a given task, rather than defaulting to "get stronger" as the only
lever.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this framework is a conceptual organizing scheme, not
a measured or validated model; the text gives no method for quantifying each of the five
components separately in a real sports movement, so treat it as a way to structure thinking
about a movement's force sources, not as a set of directly testable variables. Do not confuse
"kinesiological pattern" with a simple biomechanical description of joint angles over time;
the term is explicitly meant to include the reflexive and adaptive character of the pattern,
which a purely kinematic (position/angle) analysis would miss.

**Example** — In a vertical jump, the strength field includes the active quadriceps/glute
drive (component 1), ground reaction force (component 2), elastic energy stored during the
countermovement dip (component 3), the inertia of the body's mass being redirected (component
4), and body weight (component 5); an athlete with a weak amortization phase is likely
under-using component 3, which a purely strength-focused (component 1) training emphasis
would not fix.

# Four Ways Two Motor Abilities Can Be "Connected": General/Partial, Essential/Non-Essential, Positive/Negative, Direct/Indirect

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Verkhoshansky 1970/1972, Semyenov 1971, Tatyan 1974,
Khodykin 1976) gives a four-axis taxonomy for describing how any two motor abilities relate
to each other statistically and functionally: **general vs. partial** (a general connection
is the interaction between two abilities including the influence of all other abilities; a
partial connection isolates the interaction between just those two, controlling for others;
partial contribution is "the most typical case" lower than general, and partial connections
between the same two abilities tend to be more stable across different sports than general
ones); **essential vs. non-essential** (essential connections are those without which
efficient sporting action is impossible, and are more stable than non-essential/spurious
connections that may help or hurt efficiency incidentally); **positive vs. negative** (one
ability assists or hinders another; positive connections are most typical at the general
level, but a positive general-level connection can become negative at the partial level, e.g.
short- and long-distance running, or absolute strength versus speed of movement against small
resistance, are repeatedly found negatively connected); and **direct vs. indirect** (a direct
connection links two abilities themselves; an indirect connection links them only through a
third ability C, with no significant direct correlation between A and B themselves). (PDF pp.
144-147, printed pp. 117-120, Fig 2.23.)

**Why it works** — The author does not give a unifying physiological mechanism for why
these four connection types exist; they are presented as an empirically-derived correlational
taxonomy from factor-analytic and correlational studies of athletes across sports and
qualification levels. **Inference:** the general/partial and direct/indirect distinctions are
essentially statistical control concepts (does a relationship survive when a third variable
is accounted for), while the essential/non-essential and positive/negative distinctions
describe the practical, coaching-relevant consequence of that relationship for training
transfer.

**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy to interpret why a strength test doesn't correlate with
a performance result the way expected: a lack of a *direct* correlation does not rule out a
meaningful *indirect* connection through a mediating quality (see the worked example in
[[claim--absolute-leg-strength-connects-to-sprint-speed-only-indirectly-via-jump]]).
**Inference:** before concluding "strength doesn't matter for this skill" from a flat direct
correlation, check whether an indirect path through a more proximate quality (power, RFD,
technical efficiency) exists.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this taxonomy describes correlational patterns from
Soviet-era multi-sport samples, not a causal model; a "positive general connection" does not
establish that training ability A causes improvement in ability B, only that they co-vary
across athletes. Do not use "indirect connection" as an excuse to justify training any
quality as relevant to any outcome; the text specifically ties the useful indirect
connections to a plausible mediating mechanism (e.g. leg strength to jump height to sprint
speed, all through the shared mechanism of maximal force feeding takeoff impulse), not to an
arbitrary chain of associations.

**Example** — Absolute grip strength and 40-yard-dash time likely show a weak or negative
*direct/partial* connection (little to no useful transfer path), while absolute leg strength
and sprint speed show no useful *direct* connection but a real *indirect* one, mediated
through jumping ability (see linked claim below).

[[framework--key-specific-nonspecific-levelling-motor-ability-model]],
[[claim--physical-quality-transfer-decreases-as-specific-fitness-increases]],
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1).

# A Sprinter's Absolute Leg Strength Has No Direct Correlation With Running Speed, but Connects to It Indirectly Through Jump Performance

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky states there is no significant direct connection between
running speed and a sprinter's absolute leg strength, and that this connection is in fact
negative at the partial-correlation level (i.e., once other factors are controlled for, more
absolute leg strength is weakly associated with less speed). However, there is a real, close
connection between absolute leg strength and jumping-exercise performance, and jumping
performance is in turn closely connected to running speed, so leg strength connects to sprint
speed indirectly through jump ability (Fig 2.23b). He extends the chain further with a
worked example: there is no direct significant connection between vertical jump height (h)
and absolute leg strength (So), but absolute strength determines the maximal force of the
take-off (Fmax), which determines the impulse of the push-off (F times t), which determines
jump height. (PDF pp. 146-147, printed pp. 119-120.)

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the author gives the mechanical chain explicitly for the
jump example (absolute strength to maximal takeoff force to impulse to jump height) but does
not spell out why sprint speed itself fails to connect *directly* to leg strength; a plausible
reading, consistent with
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1), is that sprinting at speed
uses leg strength at very different joint angles, contraction velocities, and ground-contact
times than a strength test measures, so raw strength predicts the shared underlying capacity
(impulse production) better than it predicts the sport skill (running speed) directly.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against expecting a simple squat-max-to-sprint-time
correlation, and instead track a mediating measure (jump height, jump-derived impulse or
power) as the more direct bridge between weight-room strength gains and sprint performance.
**Eric's baseline:** the Baylor Sport Assessment Table already pairs strength and jump/sprint
measures within the same sport-specific battery (CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower
strength estimation, linear sprint), rather than testing strength or speed alone
(`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md`). **Inference:** this claim supports reading
jump metrics specifically as the connective tissue between a strength-training block's
results and expected sprint carryover, and argues against treating a stalled 40-yard-dash
time as evidence that more strength work is needed if jump metrics (the more directly
connected quality) haven't moved either.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab, Soviet-era correlational finding
(Verkhoshansky, 1977), not a controlled intervention study, and does not establish that
increasing absolute strength has no *causal* value for sprint speed, only that the two are
not directly, statistically connected in the samples studied; **Inference:** modern sprint
literature is genuinely mixed on how much heavy strength training transfers to sprint speed
at different training ages, and some modern sources treat this relationship as more
context-dependent (training age, starting strength level) than this passage implies; treat
this claim as one data point in that broader, still-unsettled discussion, not a settled
modern consensus. Do not use it to justify dropping strength training for speed-dependent
athletes; the mediating chain (strength to jump to speed) still requires the strength link to
function.

**Example** — A defensive back who adds significant back-squat strength but shows no change
in CMJ height or jump-derived impulse would not be expected, per this claim, to see much
carryover to sprint speed either; the more useful readiness signal for expected sprint
improvement is the jump-performance metric, not the strength-test number itself.

**Related** — [[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] (Chapter 1),
[[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]] (Chapter 1).

# The Structure of Physical Fitness: Key, Specific, Non-Specific, and Levelling Motor Abilities

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (1977) models an athlete's physical fitness as a hierarchy of
four kinds of motor ability (Fig 2.25): the **key motor ability (KMA)**, the integrated
ability that most directly determines competitive success in a given sport action, produced
by the combined development of a **specific ability (SA)** (which directly serves the key
ability's productivity) and a **non-specific ability (NSA)** (which does not itself satisfy
the sport's specific motor demand but assists when the specific ability alone is not enough,
e.g. muscular strength assisting speed of movement when external resistance is high); and
**levelling motor abilities (LMA)**, which smooth out negative correlations between the
specific and non-specific abilities, improve the connection between them, and expand the
functional range and adaptability of the key ability. Each of the specific and non-specific
abilities is itself built from a set of more basic **elementary abilities (EA)**, which stay
functionally independent and do not get "absorbed" into the key ability, but are integrated
by a **specific motor programme (SMP)** into a **specific neuromuscular structure (SNS)**
unique to that skill (worked example for explosive strength in Fig 2.26: the SMP integrates
starting-strength, absolute strength, acceleration-strength, and reactive ability into one
functional SNS). A non-specific ability can also actively hurt the key ability: the text gives
excessive absolute-strength development as an example of a non-specific ability that can
negatively affect speed. (PDF pp. 151-153, printed pp. 120-122, Figs 2.25-2.26.)

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the author does not explain the neurophysiological basis
of the SMP/SNS integration process beyond naming it; the practical logic of the model is that
sporting success rarely depends on one isolated quality, and treating "the key ability" as a
single trainable target misses that it is actually assembled from at least two different
ability types (specific and non-specific) plus a smoothing/levelling function, each of which
may need distinct types of training exposure.

**When to apply** — Use this model when auditing a training program's coverage: for a given
sport-critical key ability, identify (1) what directly-specific quality is being trained, (2)
what non-specific "helper" quality is also feeding it and whether it's being trained
appropriately (not over- or under-emphasized), and (3) whether any levelling work exists to
resolve conflicts between the specific and non-specific pieces (e.g. general conditioning or
mobility work that keeps a heavy-strength emphasis from degrading speed quality).
**Inference:** this maps onto Eric's baseline's stated training-compatibility constraint that
incompatible qualities are not trained at full intensity in the same block, and that
compatible qualities are trained together while the rest are trained at a retention dose
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29`); the levelling-ability concept here gives a
possible mechanism for why some quality combinations are compatible (a levelling ability
smooths their interaction) and others are not, though this specific mechanistic link is this
entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a conceptual model, not a measured or directly
testable one; the text gives no protocol for identifying which of an athlete's abilities are
"key" versus "non-specific" versus "levelling" in a given sport beyond correlational and
factor-analytic study of large athlete samples (see
[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]]), which most single-team programs
cannot replicate. Do not use this model to justify adding more distinct "levelling"
exercises without evidence that a specific conflict between two trained qualities actually
exists; the model describes an interaction that can occur, not one that always needs a
dedicated training solution.

**Example** — For a defensive lineman, the key motor ability might be "get-off speed and
initial force at the snap." The specific ability feeding it could be starting-strength/RFD
work; a non-specific ability assisting it could be absolute strength (helps when facing a
heavier blocker); but if heavy absolute-strength training starts to slow the athlete's
get-off (the negative-influence case named in the text), some levelling element (e.g.
continued speed-strength or reactive work alongside the strength block) would be needed to
keep the non-specific quality from degrading the key ability.

**Related** — [[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]],
[[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]] (Chapter 1).

# Transfer Between Physical Qualities (Strength, Speed, Endurance) Shrinks as an Athlete's Specific Fitness Rises

**What it is** — Summarizing a body of Soviet and Western literature (Zimkin 1956/1965;
Zatsiorsky 1961/1965; Yakovlev et al 1960; Hebb 1949; Lindeburg 1949; Nelson 1957; Woodworth
1958; Cratty 1964, 1968; Cumbeca et al 1957; Bachman 1961; Lawther 1968; Barrow 1971;
Korobkov 1958), Verkhoshansky reports several established findings on how general physical
qualities (strength, speed, endurance) relate to each other over an athlete's development:
transference of physical qualities decreases as specific fitness increases; the transfer
mechanism is largely specific rather than general; the relationship between physical
qualities can be positive, negative, or neutral; and positive transfer between qualities in
early training can turn into negative transfer later (Korobkov, 1958). He also notes it was
often claimed that complex training combining speed, strength, and endurance work develops
each quality better than training each individually (Ozolin, 1949, 1970), but states this
specific claim's validity is examined later in the book rather than settled here. (PDF pp.
139-141, printed pp. 116-117.)

**Why it works** — The author's own explanation is the conditioned-reflex model of learned
muscular activity: training builds an extensive background of "temporary connections" that
different combinations of motor activity can later draw on, and in early training these
qualities develop somewhat separately before becoming integrated through sport-specific
movements that are structurally similar to them. **Inference:** this is functionally the same
underlying idea as the more detailed ten-dimension specificity principle from Chapter 1 (see
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]), applied here at the coarser level of
whole physical qualities (strength/speed/endurance) rather than the ten specific training
dimensions within strength itself.

**When to apply** — Use this as the rationale for reducing reliance on general physical
qualities (e.g. general conditioning, general strength) as an athlete advances, and shifting
training emphasis toward sport-specific expressions of those qualities as specific fitness
rises. **Eric's baseline:** the department already sequences training from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk) rather than treating "sport specific" as a single category
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`, `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`). **Inference:**
this claim supports that same general-to-specific sequencing logic, and adds the caution that
positive transfer seen in an athlete's early training years should not be assumed to persist
unchanged as that athlete advances; a quality that helped early on can plateau in usefulness,
or even work against continued improvement, later.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the "complex training" question (whether training
speed, strength, and endurance together beats training them separately) is explicitly left
unresolved in this passage; do not cite this section as evidence for or against combined
training methods, since the author himself defers that judgment to later chapters not yet
ingested. This claim is also a summary of an older, mixed literature base spanning several
decades and traditions (1920s-1970s), not a single controlled study; treat the general
direction (transfer shrinks with rising specificity) as the useful takeaway rather than any
precise magnitude.

**Example** — A young multi-sport high-school athlete's general strength and conditioning
work is likely to transfer broadly across several sports; the same general strength and
conditioning work in a veteran college athlete already near the ceiling of his sport-specific
qualities is expected, per this claim, to transfer far less, and may need to be replaced by
increasingly sport- and position-specific training to keep producing gains.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1),
[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]] (Chapter 1).

# Strength Qualities and Muscle Groups Develop in a Fixed Order as Sports Mastery Grows, Not All at Once

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky terms "heterochronicity" the finding that, as sports mastery
grows, different strength qualities and different muscle groups develop their key role at
different times rather than simultaneously (his own coinage for the phenomenon, sourced to
his 1977 work). Two forms are described. (1) **Strength-quality order**: maximum/absolute
strength (So) increases from the start of training; explosive strength (Se) begins increasing
next, later; starting-strength (Ss) rises significantly only after that, tied to the
introduction of near-competition-intensity work (Fig 2.22a). (2) **Muscle-group order**:
which muscle group carries the "key" role for a skill shifts with mastery, e.g. in pole
vaulting, the abdominal muscles drive the initial pole-raising strength in novices, and the
shoulder flexors and elbow extensors take over that functional role as mastery grows
(Nikonov & Verkhoshansky, Fig 2.21); in the shot put, the correlation between athletic result
and arm-muscle strength drops from 0.83 (novices) to 0.73 (elite), while the correlation with
leg strength rises from 0.37 (novices) to 0.87 (elite) (Verkhoshansky & Purvin). A related
sequence is given for ankle/hip/knee starting-strength in jumpers and sprinters: ankle
flexors develop first (they bear the earliest, most intense load), followed by hip and knee
extensors, with hip flexors developing later and less intensely (they only oppose gravity and
one limb's inertia, a smaller demand). (PDF pp. 123-126, printed pp. 112-115, Figs 2.21-2.22.)

**Why it works** — For the strength-quality order, the author attributes the pattern to
which quality receives the heaviest training emphasis at each stage: absolute strength work
dominates early training, speed-strength work is introduced next, and specialized, near-
competition-intensity work (which most directly trains starting-strength) comes latest in a
periodized plan. For the muscle-group order, he attributes it to which muscle groups bear the
largest mechanical load at each stage of skill development (e.g. ankle flexors are loaded
most intensely from the very start of ground-contact-based skills, hip flexors much less so,
since they only move a single limb against gravity).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** use the strength-quality order (absolute, then explosive,
then starting-strength) as a rough sequencing guide within a periodized plan, consistent with
the classic strength-to-power progression already in Eric's baseline: **Eric's baseline:**
off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first, with
already-strong athletes shifting more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`). **Inference:** this claim adds a further,
specific step this baseline does not name: starting-strength (the ability to build force
fastest right at the onset of contraction) is described here as the *last* quality to develop
significantly, tied specifically to near-competition-intensity sport-specific work rather
than general strength or speed-strength training; a plan that stops at speed-strength work
may be leaving starting-strength underdeveloped without adding sport-specific,
near-competition-intensity exposure.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from a small number of Soviet single-sport case studies
(pole vault, shot put, plus unnamed jumpers/sprinters), not a broad multi-sport sample;
**Inference:** do not assume the exact muscle-group sequence (e.g. ankle before hip before
knee) generalizes unchanged to football-specific skills, which load the ankle, hip, and knee
in different relative proportions than pole vaulting or shot put. The strength-quality order
(absolute, then explosive, then starting-strength) is also stated to hold mainly for "sports
where the athlete overcomes relatively small resistance, and where the speed of producing
working force ... is most important" (PDF p. 143, printed p. 114), which does not obviously
describe heavy-resistance line-play skills.

**Example** — A freshman football player early in a strength program would be expected, per
this claim, to show his fastest early gains in general/absolute strength; explosive-strength
gains (jump, throw-type output) should follow once absolute strength is established; and
the sharpest gains in true starting-strength (getting off the ball fast at the snap) should
be expected latest, once near-game-intensity technical and speed work is added, not from
weight-room strength work alone.

**Related** — [[claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (Chapter 1, the
biochemical-level version of the same named phenomenon),
[[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]],
[[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]].
